\title{Discrete Trade}
\author{Ahmad Lashkaripour}
\date{\today}
\usepackage{adjustbox}
\usepackage{multirow}
\usepackage[justification=centering]{caption}

\renewcommand\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\renewcommand\theenumi\labelenumi

\usepackage[margin=15pt,font=small,labelfont={bf,sf}]{caption}
\usepackage{microtype}
\usepackage{placeins}
\usepackage{enumitem}
\usepackage{bbm}
 \usepackage{relsize}

\makeatother

\usepackage{babel}
\providecommand{\lemmaname}{Lemma}
\providecommand{\propositionname}{Proposition}

\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
\emph{International quality specialization} (IQS) and\emph{ pricing-to-market}
(PTM) are two of the most studied phenomena in international trade.
I present new evidence that PTM and IQS are significantly more pronounced
in discrete industries that involve indivisible consumption goods.
In light of this observation, I develop a generalized model of international
trade that accommodates both discrete and continuous industries. I
argue that IQS and PTM in discrete industries are magnified by $(i)$
affordability constraints, and $(ii)$ cross-country differences in
the price of non-traded services---both of which are less relevant
in continuous industries. This prediction finds support from micro-level
trade data. I then map the discrete model to macro-level data and
show that the unique forces underlying the model shed fresh light
on the gains from trade and the \textquotedblleft big-push\textquotedblright{}
effects of globalization. %
\begin{comment}

\end{comment}
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

\begin{comment}
\begin{itemize}
\item Control for differentiated goods based on the Rauch classification
\item Revise assumptions: drop bound on quality. State assumption about
buying.
\item Revise Lemmas 2 and 3
\item Discuss why continuous goods are not a substitute for services, but
rather an input in services.
\item When buying the service provided by discrete goods, consumers have
two options: $(i)$ pay the full price and benefit from the flow of
services, or $(ii)$ rent the service by paying a (near-zero) fraction
of the discrete good's price plus the labor involved in offering the
service.
\end{itemize}
\end{comment}
Around 50\% of all U.S. import transactions from 1989 to 2015 involved
\emph{discrete} goods such as ``Transport Equipment'', ``Electronics
\& Appliances,'' and ``Machinery.'' A defining feature of these
goods is that they are \textbf{\emph{indivisible}} and durable. That
is, consumers can purchase discrete goods, like cars, smartphones,
or washer-dryers, in only integer quantities. However, once purchased,
these goods supply a continuous flow of transportation, communication,
or laundry services.\footnote{Researchers often think of discrete goods as providing a flow of services:
Cars, for instance, provide a flow of transportation services, or
washer-dryer units provide a flow of dry-cleaning services---see
\citet{benhabib1991homework}, \citet{cooley1995economic}, and \citet{fernandez2011consumption},
among many others, for this analogy.}

Indivisibility of this kind has sharp implications for consumer choice.
Most importantly, consumers cannot buy a fraction of multiple discrete
goods. They are instead left with two options: $(a)$ pay the price
of one full unit, which is akin to paying a fixed acquisition cost;
or $(b)$ purchase a service that can substitute for such goods. They
can also combine these two options. For instance, a consumer may purchase
a personal vehicle for day-to-day use and spend the rest of their
transportation budget on more-specialized transportation services.
Either way and unlike what standard models assume, consumers cannot
just buy a small fraction of different varieties of cars for different
transportation demands.\footnote{There is always the option of renting or leasing multiple varieties
of a discrete good. Here, I treat that option as a type of service.
But even then, one should bear in mind that in most low-income countries
this option is not widely-accessible (see Banerjee (2003)). Also,
this option is less plausible for non-portable discrete goods such
as home appliances.}

These practical issues have received formal attention in several fields,
including \emph{industrial organization} and \emph{macroeconomics}.
Given the prevalence of discrete trade, one may also expect careful
modeling of these same issues in mainstream theories of international
trade. However, on the contrary, the issue of \emph{discreteness}
remains largely untreated in mainstream trade models.

A possible argument for this lack of attention is that discreteness
plays a less critical role when studying macro-level trade patterns.
But a basic analysis of product-level US trade data challenges this
argument. In particular, comparing discrete industries to continuous
(non-discrete) counterparts, such as ``Food,'' ``Chemicals,''
or ``Textile \& Apparel,'' indicates that
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is significantly more cross-national quality/price heterogeneity
within discrete industries;
\item There is a greater degree of international quality specialization
(IQS) in discrete industries; and 
\item There is a greater degree of pricing-to-market (PTM) in discrete industries.
\end{enumerate}
These differences remain significant, even after we control for other
characteristics like the intended final use or degree of product differentiation.
At face value, the above regularities suggest that in discrete industries,
trade patterns such as IQS and PTM are amplified by forces that are
dormant in continuous industries. Such forces are also inevitably
overlooked by mainstream theories that treat all industries or goods
as continuous. 

Motivated by this evidence, I develop a simple model of discrete trade
that pursues two objectives. First, I use the model to elucidate how
\emph{discreteness} may affect macro-level trade patterns (like IQS
and PTM) in ways that are difficult to understand from the lens of
standard trade models. Second, I use the discrete model to determine
how accounting for discrete trade revises our understanding of the
gains from trade---an issue that has received considerable attention
in the contemporary trade literature.

My theory accommodates both continuous and discrete industries. Continuous
industries are modeled in a fairly standard fashion. My modeling of
discrete industries, however, is grounded in three basic assumptions.
$(i)$ Discrete goods are indivisible, wherein purchasing them involves
paying a unit price that is akin to a fixed acquisition cost. $(ii)$
The consumption flow derived from a personally-acquired discrete good
is increasing in its quality and can be substituted with analogous
services. $(iii)$ Quality and quantity are not isomorphic: a firm
cannot produce a lower quality version of their product by employing
fewer inputs under the same production technology. Instead, any supply-side
adjustment to output quality involves paying a fixed R\&D cost.

Using the above model, I show that in \emph{discrete} industries,
IQS and PTM are magnified by two forces that are less relevant in
\emph{continuous} industries:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Cross-national heterogeneity in the price of non-traded services,
and
\item Affordability constraints, whereby consumers with a limited budget
cannot afford certain discrete varieties.
\end{enumerate}
Both of these forces operate in a somewhat similar fashion. They lead
to the \emph{market-level} demand elasticity and demand for quality
to diverge across rich and poor markets, even when \emph{individual-level}
preferences are homothetic and identical across rich and poor consumers.

The role of force $(i)$ in prompting cross-national demand differences
can be explained as follows. In each national market, discrete goods
compete head-to-head with services; but services are significantly
more expensive in high-wage economies (i.e., the Balassa-Samuelson
effect). As a result, the opportunity cost of acquiring a discrete
good is lower in high-wage markets, and this is true across all income
groups. These considerations give rise to two macro-level demand patterns.
First, the overall demand for discrete goods is \emph{less} price-elastic
in high-wage markets. Second, there is also more demand for high-quality
(high-cost) discrete varieties in these markets.

To give an example, consider a premium hair-clipper that is a discrete
tradable good. In Mumbai, India, the supplier of the hair-clipper
competes with \$5 haircut services, whereas in Oslo, Norway, it competes
with \$80 haircut services.\footnote{Source: \url{http://www.businessinsider.com/how-expensive-haircuts-are-around-the-world-2015-9}}
As a result, Indian consumers (across all income groups) will exhibit
a higher degree of price sensitivity when purchasing the hair-clipper.
The supplier will internalize this when setting their price or choosing
their output quality for these two markets.

Contrast this with continuous goods like shampoo or hair products.
Since these goods perish upon consumption, they cannot be directly
substituted with services. Instead, one has to (indirectly) pay for
them even if they use the barber service. The same goes for the gas
used in transportation services or the food used in restaurant services.
One can circumvent paying for the full price of a vehicle or a premium
grill, by taking a cab or going to a restaurant. But irrespective
of whether they use such services or operate their personal vehicle/grill,
they have to pay for the continuous perishable input, which is food
or gas in this example.

Force $(ii)$ prompts cross-national demand differences in a different
way. Since discrete goods cannot be purchased in fractional quantities
and come with a pre-customized quality, they can be unaffordable to
low-budget consumers. Consider, for example, the Toyota Corolla which,
in 2017, came with a price tag that was 8-times the annual wage rate
in India. In such circumstances, \emph{one} \noun{Toyota Corolla}
can be prohibitively expensive for a significant portion of Indian
consumers---especially given that most low-income consumers do not
have access to financing options (\citet{banerjee2003contracting}).
Correspondingly, a marginal increase in price can rule out a non-trivial
measure of potential customers.

The elasticity of demand in discrete industries, therefore, depends
on the hazard rate at which a price increase renders the product unaffordable
to marginal, low-budget consumers. This hazard rate is itself decreasing
in the discrete good's overall \emph{degree of affordability}, i.e.,
its price relative to the wage rate in the economy.\footnote{This relationship holds for any empirically-relevant income distribution,
since they exhibit an Increasing Generalized Failure Rate---see \citet{lariviere2001selling}
and \citet{lariviere2006note}.} These considerations, once again, give rise to two macro-level demand
patterns. First, the overall demand for discrete goods is \emph{less}
price-elastic in high-wage markets, where the good is on average more
affordable. Second, there is more demand for high-quality (high-cost)
varieties in these markets.

The cross-national demand differences triggered by Forces $(i)$ and
$(ii)$, can magnify the extent of PTM and IQS in \emph{discrete}
industries quite significantly. First, they prompt the suppliers of
discrete goods to set higher markups in high-wage markets where their
good is more affordable and also competes with expensive services.
Second, the \emph{affordability-driven} and \emph{service price-driven}
local demand for quality in high-wage economies prompts high-quality
specialization in these economies through scale effects. 

To test the relevance of these forces, I combine data on export prices,
export sales, and non-traded service prices for 147 countries across
5,231 6-digit (HS6) industries in the year 2011. As in the prior literature,
I document that in all industries export price levels depend systematically
on market size, income per capita, and geography. In discrete industries,
however, export prices increase with three additional factors that
are less-relevant in continuous industries: $(i)$ the price of non-traded
services in the importing market, $(ii)$ the price of non-traded
services in the exporting economy, and $(iii)$ the exporting economy's
overall cost efficiency in the industry of interest. While the empirical
significance of these additional factors confirms the predictions
of the model, the estimated effects are also quite profound. For example,
a 10\% increase in the price of services in an importing market is
associated with a 2.5\% increase in the price of \emph{discrete} imports.

On a broader level, accounting for discrete trade can revise our estimates
for the gains from trade. When the traded sector is modeled as discrete
rather than continuous, the predicted gains from trade are on average
28\% larger but more unequally distributed across countries. These
differences are driven by two factors. The first factor is somewhat
mechanical: The gains from discrete trade depend on the \emph{quantity}
share of foreign goods in national consumption, whereas the gains
from continuous trade depend on the \emph{value }share of foreign
goods in national expenditure (\citet{Arkolakis}). 

The second factor is more profound. The discrete model predicts scale-driven
gains from trade that are absent in the continuous model. To elaborate,
in the continuous model, the scale of national production in the traded
sector is invariant to trade.\footnote{More specifically, the national scale of production in the traded
sector is determined exclusively by population size. This result will
be revised if we model the traded sector as a blend of multiple industries
with different scale elasticities---see \citet{costinot2014trade}
and \citet{kucheryavyy2016grounded}.} In the discrete model, however, opening to trade induces firm-relocation
from large to small and low-income economies. This type of relocation
allows firms to collect a higher markup on marginal cost when selling
to large and rich international markets. It also expands the scale
of production in small and low-income economies at the expense of
others. 

Consider Canada, for instance, which is located close to the richer
and larger U.S. market. From the lens of the discrete model, trade-induced
scale expansion accounts for 5.6\% of Canada's real GDP. Intuitively,
trade openness induces firms to relocate from the U.S. to Canada,
using it as a platform to export to the U.S. at a higher markup. Given
the sheer size of the U.S. economy, these developments provide a sizable
boost for Canada's real GDP. They also relate to the \emph{``big-push''}
effects of economic development, wherein the growth of an economy
may be hindered by its small local market (\citet{rosenstein1943problems,lewis1954economic,murphy1989industrialization}).
But through firm-relocation, international trade can push such an
economy out of this supposed growth trap.

Aside from contributing to ongoing debates about the size and nature
of the gains from trade, the present paper contributes to our understanding
of IQS and PTM. Existing theories of IQS and PTM often model industries
as continuous.\footnote{See \citet{Schott2004,Hallak2006,choi2009explaining,Baldwin,lugovskyy2012geography,feenstra2014international,antoniades2015heterogeneous,jaimovich2015love,alcala2016specialization}
for papers studying IQS using continuous good frameworks, as well
as \citet{atkeson2008pricing,hummels2009international,bekkers2015balassa,chen2014quality,simonovska2015income,bertoletti2018international}
for papers studying PTM using continuous good frameworks.} As a result, they naturally emphasize non-homothetic preferences
and cross-national technology differences as the drivers of PTM and
IQS. Prior theories of IQS and PTM that admit discrete goods (e.g.,
\citet{Flam1987,murphy1997quality,verhoogen2008trade,Khandelwal2010,Fajgelbaum2011,dingel2016determinants,auer2018quality}),
have often $(i)$ abstracted from affordability constraints, and $(ii)$
do not include a non-traded service sector.\footnote{For instance, in the seminal work of \citet{Fajgelbaum2011}, IQS
is driven solely by non-homothetic preferences for quality, through
the home-market effect. Another closely related framework by \citet{matsuyama2000ricardian}
emphasizes a hierarchical demand system where different sectors produce
goods of different \emph{priority} as opposed to different quality. } As a result, from the lens of these models, discreteness in itself
does not contribute to IQS or PTM. Accordingly, these models cannot
explain why IQS and PTM are more pronounced in discrete industries.

\section{\label{sec:Suggestive-Evidence}Suggestive Evidence}

I uncover four new regularities, which suggest that discrete goods
account for a significant portion of global trade; and that macro-level
trade patterns such as international quality specialization (IQS)
and pricing-to-market (PTM) occur more intensively in discrete product
categories. These regularities are documented using the publicly-available
US import and export databases compiled and updated by \citeauthor{Feenstra2002}.
The data covers 36 years of US trade, reporting the f.o.b. (free on
board) value and physical quantity of district-level imports (exports)
from (to) various countries during the 1989-2015 period. Each observation
classifies the goods based on the 10-digit Harmonized System (HS10)
classification and reports the ``unit'' in which quantity is measured.\footnote{There is a small subset of observations for which the unit of measurement
is missing. Also, during the 1990-2006 period, the HS10 codes underwent
multiple revisions. So, to concord HS10 codes across revisions, I
use the mapping developed by \citet{pierce2012concordance}.} The import-side data, for instance, reports quantity in 48 different
units, with well over 70\% of the observations reporting quantity
in terms of either ``count'' or ``kilogram.'' 

My analysis in this section is complicated by two basic challenges:
First, \emph{discreteness} may be correlated with other product characteristics
such as degree of differentiation or intent of final use. Second,
\emph{discreteness} may be correlated with hidden firm-level characteristics
that are impossible to control for in the aggregate-level US data.
To address the former issue, I use the classification by \citet{Rauch1999}
to control for product differentiation and the classification of Broad
Economic Categories (BEC) to control for the intent of final use.
To address the latter concern, I cross-check all the benchmark results
with firm-level evidence. This evidence is documented using firm-level
Colombian import and export data, which report trade statistics corresponding
to individual importing and exporting firms at the HS10 level of product
aggregation during the 2007-2013 period---see Appendix \ref{sec:The-Firm-Level-Colombian}
for a more detailed description.

\vspace{0.1in}\begin{obsv}A significant portion of foreign trade
involves discrete goods.\end{obsv} \vspace{0.1in}

I classify an HS10 category as \emph{discrete} if it involves countable
goods.\footnote{A very small minority of HS10 codes report quantity in multiple units.
These observations are dropped throughout my analysis.} As reported in Table \ref{tab: Discrete Industries}, discrete HS10
products typically belong to the ``Machinery,'' ``Electrical \&
Optical Equipment,'' and ``Transport Equipment'' industries. More
than 90\% of import transactions in these industries involve discrete
goods like passenger cars, television sets, or washer/dryers. In many
widely-used classifications, these industries are also often classified
as durable. 

In comparison, industries like ``Food'', ``Chemicals'', and ``Textiles''
consist of mostly non-discrete HS10 categories. They feature products
such as coffee beans, rubbing alcohol, or yarns that typically report
quantity in kilograms. Considering that weight is a relatively continuous
unit of measurement and to fix ideas, I refer to such HS10 categories
as \emph{continuous}. 

A possible concern with the above classification is that some HS10
product codes involve countable but inexpensive goods such as flashlights.
The low unit price in these categories can render indivisibility or
discreteness redundant. So, when documenting the subsequent regularities,
I check robustness under a more conservative classification, wherein
HS10 categories are coded as discrete if they are both $(i)$ countable
and $(ii)$ exhibit an average unit price above \$1000.\footnote{In the interest of space, Regularities 3 and 4 are documented and
reported only under the benchmark classification. However, they can
be stated as is under my more conservative classification of discrete
products.}

\vspace{0.1in} \begin{obsv}
There is significantly more international price heterogeneity within discrete product categories.
\end{obsv} \vspace{0.1in}

I establish the above regularity using \emph{quantity-weighted} unit
prices, which I denote by $\bar{p}_{ji,kt}$ (origin country $j$--US
district $i$--HS10 product $k$--year $t$). Table \ref{tab:Price-Heterogeneity}
reports basic statistics describing the cross-national heterogeneity
in $\bar{p}_{ji,kt}$ within \emph{HS10 product$\times$district$\times$year}
cells. For discrete product categories, the median cell exhibits a
75/25 percentile price spread of $12.0$. For \emph{continuous} product
categories, however, the median cell exhibits a 75/25 price spread
of only $2.1$. The difference is even greater if we adopt a more
conservative definition of discreteness, whereby product categories
are classified as discrete if they are not only countable but also
exhibit an average price per good of at least $\$1000$. In that case,
the median 75/25 price spread stands at $29.3$. The same exact ranking
is borne out if we use the within-product coefficient of variation
as our measure of price heterogeneity.

The lower panel in Table \ref{tab:Price-Heterogeneity} demonstrates
that similar patterns hold even after we control for the importing
firm's characteristics. This panel reports the (within cell $ikt$)
heterogeneity in $\bar{p}_{ji,kt}$, where $i$ now indexes a Colombian
importing firm. To elaborate, firm $i$ may purchase HS10 product
$k$ in year $t$ from various origin countries indexed by $j$. The
discrete products purchased by the same firm in the same year exhibit
significantly more cross-supplier price heterogeneity than non-discrete
products.

Trade economists generally attribute such within-product price heterogeneity
to international quality and markup differences (\citet{Schott2004,Hallak2006,Baldwin,Hallak2011}).
Under this interpretation, Regularity 2 suggests that there is significantly
more international quality and markup heterogeneity in discrete product
categories. The following two regularities confirm that the greater
quality/markup heterogeneity in discrete product categories has a
systematic nature, and may be due to the greater degrees of IQS and
PTM.

\vspace{0.1in} \begin{obsv}
North-South quality specialization is more pronounced in discrete product categories.
\end{obsv} \vspace{0.1in}

To analyze quality specialization, I adopt the perspective in \citet{Schott2004}
and \citet{Hummels2005}, whereby the cross-national variation in
export prices to the same market is attributed to quality differences.\footnote{Recent theoretical advances have corroborated this interpretation.
Most notably, \citet{arkolakiselusive} show that (if the firm-level
productivity distribution is Pareto), the distribution of markups
from country $j$ to $i$ is invariant to country $j$'s characteristics.
That being the case, the cross-exporter variation in prices can be
entirely attributed to export quality differences. } Correspondingly, I define the degree of North-South quality specialization
as $\frac{\partial\ln\textrm{export unit price}}{\partial\ln\textrm{origin's GDP p/c}}$.
To determine how product discreteness influences North-South quality
specialization, I run the following regression on the US import data:\footnote{\citet{manova2012export} adopt a similar estimating equation to analyze
the within-product heterogeneity in unit prices, but with firm-level
data.}
\begin{equation}
\log\bar{p}_{ji,kt}=\left(\beta_{w}+\beta_{w}^{\mathcal{D}}\times\mathbbm{1}\left\{ \textrm{Discrete}\right\} \right)\log\textrm{GDP p/c}_{j,t}+\textrm{Controls}_{j,t}+\delta_{ikt}+\epsilon_{jikt},\label{eq: QS}
\end{equation}
The dependent variable, $\bar{p}_{ji,kt}$ denotes the unit price
of country $j$'s exports to US district $i$ in HS10 product category
$k$, in year $t$. On the right-hand side, $\textrm{GDP p/c}_{j,t}$
controls for the \emph{origin }country's GDP per capita; $\mathbbm{1}\left\{ \textrm{Discrete}\right\} $
is a dummy variable that assumes a value of $1$ if product category
$k$ is discrete and is zero otherwise; $\textrm{Controls}_{j,t}$
is composed of a set of standard gravity controls like total GDP,
geo-distance, and Free Trade Agreements; and finally, $\delta_{ikt}$
controls for district-product-year fixed effects. 

In addition to estimating Equation \ref{eq: QS} on the entire sample,
I perform the same estimation while restricting the sample to $(i)$
only final consumption goods, and $(ii)$ only differentiated goods
as classified by \citet{Rauch1999}. Doing so removes the possible
concern that discreteness is correlated with other characteristics
like the intended use or the degree of product differentiation. Also,
since each observation in my country-level data represents a quantity-weighted
average of firm-level variables, the above estimation is subject to
the classic heteroskedasticity problem. To attain consistent estimates,
I follow \citet{kmenta1997elements} and weigh each observation by
the underlying trade quantity.\footnote{When handling grouped data, the weighted estimator where each observation
is weighted by the square root of group size is BLUE. Here, trade
quantity serves as a theory-consistent proxy for group size. Adopting
such a weighting scheme delivers consistent estimates even if group
size is correlated with $\epsilon_{jikt}$---see \citet{solon2015we}.} To account for sample selection, I use the two-step correction developed
by \citet{wooldridge1995selection}.\footnote{Specifically, I estimate an analog of Regression \ref{eq: QS} by
Tobit, but with trade values as the dependent variable. The residual
from this first regression is then used as an additional control when
estimating Equation \ref{eq: QS}---see \citet{harrigan2015export}
for further details.}

In the above regression, the coefficient $\beta_{w}$ reflects the
baseline degree of North-South quality specialization, while $\beta_{w}^{\mathcal{D}}$
reflects the extent to which this kind of specialization is more pronounced
in discrete product categories. The estimation results reported in
Table \ref{tab:Quality-Specialization} point to a positive and statistically
significant $\beta_{w}^{\mathcal{D}}$, indicating that IQS is noticeably
more pronounced in discrete product categories. This remains to be
true if we confine our sample to only final consumption goods or differentiated
goods.\footnote{The Weighted OLS estimator may not correct for the overrepresentation
of observations with extreme values of the explanatory variables (\citet{solon2015we}).
Nonetheless, dropping observations with explanatory variables that
fall above/below the 95/5 percentile does not qualitatively change
any of the conclusions deduced from my analysis. }

The bottom panel in Table \ref{tab:Quality-Specialization} documents
the same pattern while controlling for firm-level characteristics.
The results in this panel correspond to an estimation of Equation
\ref{eq: QS} on the firm-level Colombian import data, in which case
index $i$ indexes an importing firm rather than a district. These
results indicate that IQS is more pronounced in discrete product categories
even after we control for \emph{importing firm-product-year }fixed
effects and divide goods by degree of differentiation and intent of
final use.

The above claims rest on an implicitly-assumed link between quality
and unit price, which can be complicated by cross-national productivity
differences. Specifically, the results in Table \ref{tab:Quality-Specialization}
can be alternatively interpreted as high-income countries having a
comparative cost advantage in continuous industries. I discuss this
issue more elaborately in Section \ref{sec:Empirical-Evidence}, where
I analyze the role of discreteness while controlling for cross-country
productivity differences as well as other confounding factors. 

\vspace{0.1in} \begin{obsv}
Pricing-to-market is more pronounced in discrete product categories.
\end{obsv} \vspace{0.1in}

To analyze PTM, I adopt the perspective in \citet{alessandria2011pricing}
and \citet{simonovska2015income}, whereby the cross-market variation
in prices from the same exporter is attributed to markup differences.\footnote{Alternatively, the same pattern can be attribute to firm varying their
quality across markets. In that case, Regularity 4 can be stated as
firms vary their product quality more intensively

discrete industries. } Accordingly, I define the degree of PTM as $\frac{\partial\ln\textrm{export unit price}}{\partial\ln\textrm{destination's GDP p/c}}$.
To determine how discreteness influences PTM, I run the following
regression on the US export data:
\begin{align}
\log\bar{p}_{ji,kt} & =\left(\tilde{\beta}_{w}+\tilde{\beta}_{w}^{\mathcal{D}}\times\mathbbm{1}\left\{ \textrm{Discrete}\right\} \right)\log\textrm{GDP p/c}_{i,t}+\textrm{Controls}_{i,t}+\delta_{jkt}+\epsilon_{jikt}\label{eq: PTM}
\end{align}
The dependent variable, $\bar{p}_{ji,kt}$, denotes the unit price
of US district $j$'s exports to country $i$ in HS10 category $k$,
in year $t$. On the right-hand side, $\textrm{GDP p/c}_{i,t}$ controls
for the \emph{destination} country's GDP per capita, $\mathbbm{1}\left\{ \textrm{Discrete}\right\} $
is a discrete product dummy; $\textrm{Controls}_{i,t}$ is composed
of a set of standard gravity controls like total GDP, geo-distance,
and Free Trade Agreements; and finally, $\delta_{jkt}$ controls for
district- product-year fixed effects. Also, as before, I estimate
Equation \ref{eq: PTM} separately for all goods as well the subset
of final consumption goods and differentiated goods.

In the above regression, $\tilde{\beta}_{w}$ reflects the baseline
degree of PTM, while $\tilde{\beta}_{w}^{\mathcal{D}}$ reflects the
extent to which PTM is more pronounced in discrete product categories.
The estimation results reported in Table \ref{tab:Pricing-to-Market}
point to a positive and statistically significant $\tilde{\beta}_{w}^{\mathcal{D}}$,
indicating that PTM is in fact noticeably more pronounced in discrete
product categories. This also remains to be true if we confine our
sample to only final consumption goods or differentiated goods.

same pattern while controlling for firm-level characteristics. The
results in this panel are derived by estimating Equation \ref{eq: PTM}
on the firm-level Colombian export data, in which case index $j$
identifies an exporting firm rather than a district.\footnote{In the Colombia sample numerous firms supply both discrete and continuous
goods. To give an example, firm \#900500347 exports both durometers
(HS9024800000) that are discrete and priced over \$500 per unit as
well as continuous aluminum sheets (HS7616999000).} They indicate that PTM is more pronounced in discrete product categories
even after we control for \emph{exporting firm-product-year }fixed
effects and divide goods by degree of differentiation and intent of
final use.

To take stock, the evidence presented in this section indicate that
IQS and PTM are more pronounced in discrete industries. One possible
reason for this is that the standard drivers of IQS and PTM operate
more forcefully in discrete industries. Another possibility is that
\emph{discreteness} gives rise to alternative driving forces behind
IQS and PTM that are otherwise irrelevant. In what follows, I present
a theoretical framework that highlights two such alternative forces.

\section{\label{sec:Theoretical-Framework}Theoretical Framework}

My main objective in this section is to highlight two alternative
drivers of IQS and PTM in discrete industries. Considering this objective,
my theory purposely abstracts from \emph{taste-driven} or \emph{cost-driven}
IQS and PTM, which have little to do with discreteness. Accordingly,
I model continuous industries in a rather standard fashion. My modeling
of discrete industries and the insights that derive from it, however,
rests on three distinctive assumptions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Discrete goods are indivisible: purchasing them requires paying the
price of one full unit, which is akin to paying a fixed acquisition
cost.
\item The consumption flow derived from a personally-acquired discrete good
can be substituted with analogous services---e.g., consumers can
forgo buying a truck for moving purposes by renting a moving service.\footnote{This feature can be attributed to the strong overlap between discreteness
and durability (see Section \ref{sec:Suggestive-Evidence}). Unlike
perishable consumption goods, durable consumption goods are non-rival.
That is, one consumer's usage of the good does not exclude others
from using it later. Accordingly, one can use a taxi service without
(effectively) paying for the car but by only paying for the labor
and the perishable fuel used in providing the service. This feature
of durable goods has been widely-invoked in macro-economics literature---see
\citet{benhabib1991homework}, \citet{cooley1995economic}, and \citet{fernandez2011consumption}.}
\item Quality and quantity are not isomorphic. In particular, from the perspective
of a firm, supplying higher quality is different from supplying more
quantity. The former requires incurring a sunk R\&D cost, whereas
the latter only requires employing more inputs without necessarily
altering one's production technology.
\end{enumerate}
For the sake of composition, I also make various parametric assumptions
throughout this section; but these assumptions are less consequential
to the theoretical results that follow---Appendix \ref{sec: Non-Parametric-Model}
shows that the main predictions of the model hold equally in a more
general (less-parametric) environment. 

\subsection{Economic Environment}

\paragraph*{\emph{Countries.}}

The global economy consists of $i=1,...,I$ countries, with $\mathbb{C}$
denoting the set of countries. Country $i$ is populated by $L_{i}$
individuals, each of whom is endowed with $y\in\mathbb{R_{+}}$ units
of effective labor that is the sole factor of production. All individuals
are perfectly mobile across the production of different goods but
are immobile across countries; and are paid an economy-wide wage,
$w_{i}$, per unit of effective labor. 

\paragraph*{\emph{Income Distribution.}}

I assume that the distribution of effective labor, $y$, across individuals
within country $i$ is given by
\[
G_{i}(y)=1-e^{-\zeta_{i}\left(y-\bar{y}_{i}\right)}.
\]
Since each individual residing in country $i$ collects an income
equal to $yw_{i}$, then $G_{i}\left(.\right)$ also governs the distribution
of income in that country. The exponential parametrization of the
income distribution is motivated by evidence in \citet{druagulescu2001evidence}
and \citet{gabaix2009power}. I allow parameters $\zeta_{i}$ and
$\bar{y}_{i}$ to vary arbitrarily across countries; but I impose
that the mean of the distribution equals one in all countries, i.e.,
$\mathbb{E}_{i}(y)=\bar{y}_{i}+\zeta_{i}=1$ for all $y$. 

\paragraph*{\emph{Industries.}}

The economy is composed of multiple industries (indexed by $k$) that
fall under three general categories:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Continuous industries, which involve traded and \emph{infinitely-divisible}
goods, with $\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}$ denoting the set of all continuous
industries
\item Discrete industries, which involve traded but \emph{indivisible} goods,
with $\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}$ denoting the set of all discrete
industries.
\item Non-traded service industries that supply a homogeneous output, which
serves as a substitute for discrete goods. 
\end{enumerate}
I hereafter use the \emph{tilde} notation to distinguish variables
corresponding to the service sector. For instance, based on this choice
of notation, $\tilde{p}_{i,k}$ denotes the price of industry $k$-related
services in market $i$.

\paragraph*{\emph{Product Space.}}

Traded goods (whether continuous or discrete) are horizontally and
vertically differentiated. That is, they come in different firm-level
varieties (indexed by $\omega$) and different quality tiers (indexed
by $\varphi$). The set of admissible quality tiers in each industry
is predetermined and denoted by $\varPhi_{k}$. As in \citet{Fajgelbaum2011},
firms sort into (only one) of these predetermined quality tiers and
supply their differentiated variety in that particular quality level. 

In such a setup, the firm index $\omega$ uniquely identifies not
only the supplying firm but also the quality of the variety supplied
by that firm. To be more specific, let $\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)$ denote
the set of all firms supplying quality $\varphi$ from country $j$
in industry $k$. Then, if $\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)$ it is
automatically implied that $\omega\notin\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi')$ for
any $\varphi'\neq\varphi$. In that regard, the index $\omega$ implicitly
conveys full information about quality as well as industry and country
of origin.

\subsection{Demand and Supply in Continuous Industries}

I start by describing the supply and demand structure in continuous
industries. Given its standard underpinning, the continuous model
can also serve as a useful benchmark to better understand my less-standard
model of discrete industries.\vspace{-0.15in}

\paragraph*{\emph{Demand.}}

The demand structure is similar to \citet{Krugman1980}, except that
there are multiple quality tiers to choose from. In particular, each
individual spends a constant fraction, $e_{k}$, of their income on
industry $k$ goods.\footnote{To be specific, the welfare of individual $\iota$ is a Cobb-Douglas
aggregate of the industry specific utility levels. Namely, $W_{\iota}=\prod_{k\in\mathbb{K}}U_{\iota,k}^{e_{k}}$.} The budget allocated to \emph{continuous} industry $k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}$
can be spent on buying a fractional quantity of various firm-level
varieties. An individual's utility from consuming a basket $\boldsymbol{q}=\{q_{ji,k}(\omega)\}$
of firm-level varieties is given by a nested-CES function,\footnote{Implicit in the above formulation is that markets are segmented. Without
this assumption, PTM and the possibility of international arbitrage
may lead to zero trade between countries---see \citet{foellmi2017international}.}
\[
U_{k}\left(\boldsymbol{q}\right)=\left(\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}\left[\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)}\varphi^{\frac{1}{1+\theta_{k}}}\ q_{ji,k}(\omega)^{\frac{\theta_{k}}{1+\theta_{k}}}\right]^{\frac{1+\theta_{k}}{\theta_{k}}\frac{\gamma_{k}}{1+\gamma_{k}}}\right)^{\frac{1+\gamma_{k}}{\gamma_{k}}},\ \ \ k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}
\]
where $\gamma_{k}$ and $\theta_{k}>0$ reflect the degree of within-
and cross-quality substitutability between different firm-level varieties.
Utility maximization subject to the budget constraints, $\sum_{\varphi}\sum_{j}\sum_{\omega}p_{ji,k}(\omega)q_{ji,k}(\omega)\leq e_{k}w_{i}y_{\iota}$
implies that the share of spending on variety $\omega$ is independent
of personal income and given by,
\begin{equation}
\lambda_{ji,k}(\omega)=\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)^{-\theta_{k}}}{\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{\ell,k}(\varphi)}p_{\ell i,k}(\omega')^{-\theta_{k}}}\times e_{i,k}(\varphi),\ \ \ \forall\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)\label{eq: lambda cont.}
\end{equation}
where $e_{i,k}(\varphi)$ is the total share of spending on quality
$\varphi$:
\[
e_{i,k}(\varphi)=\frac{\left(\varphi\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{\ell,k}(\varphi)}p_{\ell i,k}(\omega)^{-\theta_{k}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}/\theta_{k}}}{\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}\left(\varphi'\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{\ell,k}(\varphi')}p_{\ell i,k}(\omega)^{-\theta_{k}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}/\theta_{k}}},\ \ \ \forall\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}.
\]
Accordingly, total demand for variety $\omega$ in market $i$ can
be expressed as,
\begin{equation}
q_{ji,k}(\omega)=\lambda_{ji,k}(\omega)e_{k}w_{i}L_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\label{eq: Demand Contin.}
\end{equation}
where $w_{i}L_{i}$ is total income in market $i$---the fact that
total income equals $w_{i}L_{i}$ derives from my earlier choice of
normalization, $\mathbb{E}_{i}(y)=1$.\vspace{-0.15in}

\paragraph*{\emph{Supply.}}

The supply-side of the economy is similar to \citeauthor{Fajgelbaum2011}'s
\citeyearpar{Fajgelbaum2011} extension of \citet{Krugman1980}. That
is, labor is the sole factor of production. Firms supplying goods
of the same quality (in industry $k$) are symmetric within each country,
and compete under monopolistic competition--as shown in Appendix
\ref{sec: Discrete-Trade-with-Firm-Het} the model can be easily extended
to account for firm heterogeneity. A typical firm $\omega$ supplying
quality $\varphi$ from country $j$ has to incur a sunk entry cost,
$w_{j}f_{k}^{e}(\varphi)$. It also incurs a marginal cost for each
unit of output produced and transported to market $i$ that is given
by
\[
c_{ji,k}(\omega)=\tau_{ji,k}a_{j,k}c(\varphi)w_{j}.\ \ \ \omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\omega)
\]
In the above cost specification $\tau_{ji,k}$ denotes the iceberg
transport cost; $a_{j,k}$ is a quality-neutral (\emph{country$\times$industry}-specific)
cost shifter; and $c(\varphi)$ is a universal cost shifter that accounts
for high-quality output being more costly to produce in every country.
An important feature of the above parametrization is that it precludes
any Ricardian comparative advantage along the quality margin.

The variable profit collected by a typical firm $\omega$ is, thus,
given by
\[
\pi_{ji,k}(\omega)=\left[p_{ji,k}(\omega)-c_{ji,k}(\omega)\right]q_{ji,k}(\omega),
\]
where $q_{ji,k}(\omega)$ is determined by Equation \ref{eq: Demand Contin.}.
Firms choose their optimum price, $p_{ji,k}(\omega)$, by maximizing
$\pi_{ji,k}(\omega)$, which implies a standard monopoly markup over
marginal cost. The number of firms supplying quality $\varphi$ from
country $j$ (namely, $N_{j,k}(\varphi)$) is then determined by the
\emph{free-entry} condition, wherein firms enter until net profits
are drawn to zero in every quality tier of industry $k$:
\[
\sum_{i\in\mathbb{C}}\pi_{ji,k}(\omega)=w_{j}f_{k}^{e}(\varphi),\ \ \ \forall\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi).
\]


\subsection{Demand and Supply in Discrete Industries}

Discrete industries involve goods that are \emph{indivisible} and
substitutable with analogous services. I use a discrete choice framework
to model consumer demand in these industries. On the supply-side,
though, I assume that discrete industries are identical to continuous
counterparts.\vspace{-0.15in}

\paragraph*{\emph{Demand}.}

To draw consumption utility from a discrete variety $\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)$,
consumers have to pay the unit price, $p_{ji,k}(\omega)$, which is
akin to paying a fixed acquisition cost. After the good is acquired,
it delivers a flow of consumption quantity, $q_{k}(\varphi)$, that
is increasing in the good's quality, $\varphi$. The flow of personal
consumption provided by a discrete good (like a car) is substitutable
with analogous services (like a taxi service). Consumers can, therefore,
circumvent paying the acquisition cost altogether, or they can purchase
a cheaper (lower-$\varphi$) discrete variety and complement it with
a range of specialized services.

Suppose individual $\iota$ purchases discrete variety $\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)$
(a firm-level variety of quality $\varphi$ originating from country
$j$) for personal use and combines it with $\tilde{q}_{k}$ hours
of service. The utility they derive from this choice is given by
\[
U_{\iota}(\omega,\tilde{q})=\tilde{q}_{k}+q_{k}(\varphi)+\xi_{\iota}(\omega),\ \ \ \omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)
\]
where $q_{k}(\varphi)$ (as defined earlier) denotes the consumption
quantity derived from a personally-acquired unit of good $\omega$;
and $\xi^{\iota}(\omega)$ is an \emph{individual$\times$variety}-specific
utility shifter that accounts for individual $\iota$'s personal taste
for variety $\omega$. Implicit in the above parametrization is the
fact that the consumption derived from a discrete good is perfectly
substitutable with analogous services. Without loss of generality,
I henceforth impose that $q_{k}(\varphi)=\varphi$.

As is common in the literature, I assume that the vector $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\iota,k}\equiv\left\{ \xi_{\iota}(\omega)\right\} $,
which describes individual $\iota$'s taste with respect to various
industry $k$ varieties, is drawn independently from a General Extreme
Value distribution: $F_{k}(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\iota,k})=\exp\left(-\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}\left(\sum_{\omega}\exp(\xi_{\iota}(\omega))^{-\theta_{k}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}/\theta_{k}}\right)$,
where $\theta_{k}\geq\gamma_{k}\geq0$ are parameters governing the
heterogeneity of consumer taste within and across quality levels in
industry $k$. This assumption allows me to obtain closed-form demand
functions.

An individual (with endowment $y$) maximizes their utility by choosing
their preferred variety, $\omega$, within industry $k$ subject to
a personal budget constraint. Recall that a fraction $e_{k}$ of an
individual's income is spent on industry $k$ goods/services (e.g.,
transportation goods and services). The budget constraint imposes
that the price of variety $\omega$ not exceed one's budget, $e_{k}w_{i}y$.
Moreover, given the choice of $\omega$, the budget constraint implicitly
determines their choice of service consumption, $\tilde{q}_{k}$.
That is, if an individual chooses variety $\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)$,
their budget constraint,
\[
\widetilde{p}_{i,k}\widetilde{q}_{k}+p_{ji,k}(\omega)=e_{k}w_{i}y,
\]
implicitly pins down $\tilde{q}_{k}=\left[e_{k}w_{i}y-p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right]/\tilde{p}_{i,k}$.
Taking into account the individual's budget constraint and appealing
to the Theorem of Extreme Value, utility maximization then implies
that the share of individuals with endowment $y$ who choose variety
$\omega$ is given by
\begin{equation}
\lambda_{ji,k}(\omega;y)=\frac{\exp\left(p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)^{-\theta_{k}/\tilde{p}_{i,k}}}{\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{\ell,k}(\varphi,y)}\exp\left(-p_{\ell i,k}(\omega')\right)^{-\theta_{k}/\tilde{p}_{i,k}}}\times e_{i,k}(\varphi;y),\label{eq: lambda disc.}
\end{equation}
if $y\geq\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}}$; and is zero otherwise
(see Appendix \ref{sec:Proof-of-Lemma 1} for proof). The share of
individuals with endowment $y$ who choose a variety with quality
$\varphi$ is similarly given by
\[
e_{i,k}(\varphi;y)=\frac{\left[\varphi\ \sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{\ell,k}(\varphi,y)}\exp\left(-p_{\ell i,k}(\omega)\right)^{-\theta_{k}/\tilde{p}_{i,k}}\right]^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}}}{\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}\left[\varphi'\ \sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{\ell,k}(\varphi',y)}\exp\left(-p_{\ell i,k}(\omega)\right)^{-\theta_{k}/\tilde{p}_{i,k}}\right]^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}}},
\]
where $\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi,y)\subset\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)$ denotes
the subset of varieties in set $\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)$ that are affordable
to individuals with endowment $y$. The total demand facing firm $\omega$
can, therefore, be calculated as the sum of the demand across all
individuals in the economy as follows:
\begin{equation}
q_{ji,k}(\omega)=\left(\int_{y=\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}}}^{\infty}\lambda_{ji,k}(\omega;y)dG_{i}(y)\right)L_{i}.\label{eq: Demand Discrete}
\end{equation}
Before moving forward let me draw a brief comparison between the demand
structure in discrete and continuous industries. In both sets of industries,
individual-level preferences are homothetic in the following sense.
If two individuals have different income levels (namely, $y'$ and
$y$) but can choose from the same set of varieties, then
\[
\lambda_{ji,k}(\varphi,y)=\lambda_{ji,k}(\varphi,y').
\]
Moreover, if the above condition is satisfied, it automatically follows
that the two individuals also exhibit the same demand for quality:
$e_{i,k}(\varphi,y)=e_{i,k}(\varphi,y')$. \vspace{-0.15in}

\paragraph*{\emph{Supply.}}

On the supply side, discrete industries are assumed to be identical
to continuous industries. That is, labor is the only factor of production
and firms compete under monopolistic competition. Each firm in country
$j$ incurs a sunk cost, $w_{j}f_{k}^{e}(\varphi)$, to enter industry
$k$ in quality tier $\varphi$. Upon entry, it also incurs a marginal
cost equal to $c_{ji,k}(\omega)=\tau_{ji,k}a_{j,k}c(\varphi)w_{j}$
in order to supply each unit of output to market $i$. Recall that
this cost structure rules out Ricardian comparative advantage along
the quality margin. Each firm sets their optimum price by maximizing
their variable profit,
\[
\pi_{ji,k}(\omega)=\left[p_{ji,k}(\omega)-c_{ji,k}(\omega)\right]q_{ji,k}(\omega),
\]
where $q_{ji,k}(\omega)$ is now given by Equation \ref{eq: Demand Discrete}.
Profit maximization simply entails a standard monopoly markup over
marginal cost. The number of firms in every quality tier of industry
$k$ is determined by the \emph{free-entry} condition, wherein firms
enter until net profits are drawn to zero: $\sum_{i\in\mathbb{C}}\pi_{ji,k}(\omega)=w_{j}f_{k}^{e}(\varphi)$. 

It is important to note that the production of quality is subject
to scale economies in all industries. That is, the average cost of
supplying quality is decreasing in total output. As a result, to circumvent
trade costs, high-quality firms agglomerate in economies where there
is a relatively large local demand for high-quality varieties, leading
to the well-known \emph{home-market} effect.

\subsection{Demand and Supply of Non-Traded Services}

The demand for non-traded services is implicitly determined by the
consumption choice in discrete industries.\footnote{This is a simplifying but innocuous assumption. One can always assume
that the economy features an extra set of non-traded service industries
that are unrelated to discrete industries. Adding this feature, as
long as we maintain the Cobb-Douglas assumption on industry-level
expenditure shares, will not change any of the results in the paper. } I also assume that the service sector is perfectly competitive. In
principle, services may employ discrete goods as an intermediate input
(e.g., taxi services use cars as an input), but I assume that due
to repeated use, the fixed cost paid for acquiring the discrete good
constitutes a negligible fraction of the total cost.\footnote{Specifically, consider an incumbent firm supplying \emph{industry
$k$-related} services in market $i$. Suppose such a firm spends
$\tilde{c}_{i,k}^{\mathcal{D}}$ on purchasing discrete input varieties
and sells in total $\tilde{Q}_{i,k}$ units of services. The implicit
assumption here is that $\tilde{c}_{i,k}^{\mathcal{D}}/\tilde{Q}_{i,k}\approx0$,
so that the average cost for this supplier is approximately equal
to the marginal cost: $\tilde{AC}_{i}=\tilde{a}_{i,k}w_{i}+\frac{\tilde{c}_{i,k}^{\mathcal{D}}}{\tilde{Q}_{i,k}}\approx\tilde{a}_{i,k}w_{i}.$} Consequently, the average cost, effectively, equals the marginal
cost, $\tilde{a}_{i,k}w_{i}$, for service suppliers.

I also assume that the marginal labor cost of supplying services is
the same across all industries, i.e., $\tilde{a}_{i,k}=\tilde{a}_{i,g}$
for all $g$ and $k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}$. Altogether, these
assumptions imply that the competitive price of services in market
$i$ equals:
\[
\tilde{p}_{i,k}=\tilde{p}_{i}=\tilde{a}_{i}w_{i}\ \ \ \forall k.
\]
The above equation indicates that $\tilde{p}_{i}$ and the local wage
rate, $w_{i}$, are positively but not perfectly correlated.\footnote{The positive relation between $\tilde{p}_{i}$ and $w_{i}$ is contingent
on $\tilde{a}_{i}$'s being sufficiently homogeneous across countries.
This condition serves as the foundation of the celebrated \emph{Blasssa-Samuelson
effect} (\citet{bhagwati1984services,samuelson1994facets}). } We can actually construct many theory-consistent examples where the
price of non-traded services differ across two markets with the same
$w_{i}$. This distinction plays an important role when testing the
model, later in Section \ref{sec:Empirical-Evidence}.

\subsection{Equilibrium}

In equilibrium, each firm $\omega$ that supplies quality $\varphi$
from country $j$ in industry $k$ (i.e., $\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}$)
charges the same price and sells the same quantity of output. Considering
this, I can express all variables as a function of quality rather
than the firm-level index, $\omega$. In that case, $p_{ji,k}(\varphi)$
denotes the price charged in market $i$ by a typical firm $\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)$.
With this choice of notation, I now present the main equilibrium outcomes
and formally define the equilibrium. 

Following Equations \ref{eq: lambda cont.} and \ref{eq: lambda disc.},
the market share of origin $j$ varieties in country $i$ can be expressed
as\footnote{Note that in the case of continuous industries, $\lambda_{ji,k}(\varphi)$
denotes the \emph{value-share} of spending; whereas in the case of
discrete industries, it denotes the \emph{quantity-share}.}
\begin{equation}
\lambda_{ji,k}(\varphi)=\begin{cases}
\frac{N_{j,k}(\varphi)p_{ji,k}(\varphi)^{-\theta_{k}}}{\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}N_{\ell,k}(\varphi)p_{\ell i,k}(\varphi)^{-\theta_{k}}}\times e_{i,k}(\varphi;y) & \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}\\
\int_{y=\frac{p_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{e_{k}w_{i}}}^{\infty}\frac{N_{j,k}(\varphi)\exp\left(p_{ji,k}(\varphi)\right)^{-\frac{\theta_{k}}{\tilde{p}_{i}}}}{\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}_{i}(\varphi,y)}N_{\ell,k}(\varphi)\exp\left(p_{\ell i,k}(\varphi)\right)^{-\frac{\theta_{k}}{\tilde{p}_{i}}}}\times e_{i,k}(\varphi;y)\ dG_{i}(y) & \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}
\end{cases}\label{eq: expenditure share}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}$ denotes the \textbf{\emph{set of
continuous industries}}; $\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}$ denotes the \textbf{\emph{set
of discrete industries}}; and $\mathbb{C}_{i}(\varphi,y)\in\mathbb{C}$
denotes the subset of countries whose quality $\varphi$ varieties
are affordable to income group $y$ in market $i$. The share of quality
$\varphi$ in total consumption is, meanwhile, given by:
\[
e_{i,k}(\varphi;y)=\begin{cases}
\frac{\left(\varphi\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}N_{\ell,k}(\varphi)p_{\ell i,k}(\varphi)^{-\theta_{k}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}/\theta_{k}}}{\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}\left(\varphi'\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}N_{\ell,k}(\varphi')p_{\ell i,k}(\varphi')^{-\theta_{k}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}/\theta_{k}}} & \textrm{\textrm{if }k\ensuremath{\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}}}\\
\frac{\left(\varphi\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}(\varphi,y)}N_{\ell,k}(\varphi)\exp\left(p_{\ell i,k}(\varphi)\right)^{-\frac{\theta_{k}}{\tilde{p}_{i}}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}/\theta_{k}}}{\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}\left(\varphi'\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}_{i}(\varphi,y)}N_{\ell,k}(\varphi')\exp\left(p_{\ell i,k}(\varphi')\right)^{-\frac{\theta_{k}}{\tilde{p}_{i}}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}/\theta_{k}}} & \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}
\end{cases}.
\]
The above expressions immediately imply that the equilibrium demand
elasticity facing individual firms can be stated as (see Appendix
\ref{sec: Proof-Lemma3} for derivation):
\begin{equation}
\varepsilon_{ji,k}(\varphi)=\begin{cases}
\theta_{k}+1 & \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}\\
\theta_{k}\frac{p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)}{\tilde{p}_{i}}+\zeta_{i}\frac{p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)}{e_{k}w_{i}} & \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}
\end{cases}.\label{eq: Eq epsilon}
\end{equation}
The difference between the demand elasticity faced by firms in discrete
versus continuous industries plays a key role in my theory. So, I
will discuss these differences more elaborately in the following Subsection.
Finally, given the expression for $\lambda_{ji,k}(\varphi)$, aggregate
trade values, $X_{ji,k}(\varphi)\equiv N_{j,k}(\varphi)p_{ji,k}(\varphi)q_{ji,k}(\varphi)$,
are given by
\begin{equation}
X_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)=\begin{cases}
\lambda_{ji,k}(\varphi)e_{k}Y_{i} & \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}\\
\lambda_{ji,k}(\varphi)\frac{p_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{w_{i}}Y_{i} & \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}
\end{cases},\label{eq: EQ trade values}
\end{equation}
where $Y_{i}\equiv w_{i}L_{i}$. Equilibrium corresponds to a vector
of prices, $\boldsymbol{p}\equiv\{p_{ji,k}(\varphi)\}$, wage rates,
$\boldsymbol{w}\equiv\{w_{j}\}$, and the number of firms, $\boldsymbol{N}\equiv\{N_{j,k}(\varphi)\}$,
that satisfy $(i)$ the optimal monopoly pricing condition (MP), $(ii)$
the balanced trade condition (BT), and $(iii)$ the free entry condition
(FE):
\[
\begin{cases}
p_{ji,k}(\varphi)=\frac{\varepsilon_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)}{\varepsilon_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)-1}\tau_{ji,k}a_{j,k}c(\varphi)w_{j} & \forall\varphi\in\varPhi_{k},k\in\mathbb{K}\ \ \ (\textrm{MP})\\
\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{K}}\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}X_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{k\in\mathbb{K}}\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}X_{i\ell,k}\left(\varphi\right) & \forall k\in\mathbb{K}\ \ \ (\textrm{BT})\\
N_{j,k}(\varphi)w_{j}f_{k}^{e}(\varphi)=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{C}}X_{ji,k}(\varphi)/\varepsilon_{ji,k}(\varphi) & \forall k\in\mathbb{K}\ \ \ (\textrm{FE})
\end{cases},
\]
By Walras' law, the satisfaction of the BT and FE conditions ensures
that labor markets also clear in each country.

\subsection{Discussion: \emph{The Demand Elasticity Facing Discrete Goods}}

While I assumed that individual preferences for traded goods are homothetic,
the market-level demand elasticity facing discrete goods varies systematically
across markets. This variation is driven by $(i)$ cross-market heterogeneity
in the price of non-traded services, and $(ii)$ affordability constraints
being more-or-less binding in different markets. To elaborate on these
two channels, we can decompose the demand elasticity facing discrete
goods in market $i$ as follows:

\[
\varepsilon_{ji,k}(\varphi)=\underbrace{\theta_{k}\frac{p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)}{\tilde{p}_{i}}}_{\textrm{NT-driven}}\ +\ \underbrace{\zeta_{i}\frac{p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)}{e_{k}w_{i}}}_{\textrm{affordability-driven}}.
\]
In the above expression, the \emph{NT-driven} component accounts for\emph{
}cross-country differences in the price of non-traded services. This
component depends on $(a)$ the degree of product differentiation
$\theta_{k}$, the role of which is well understood, as well as $(b)$
$p_{ji,k}(\omega)/\tilde{p}_{i}$, which is the amount of service
consumption one forgoes to acquire a full unit of variety $\omega$.
Importantly, the demand elasticity is lower the higher the price of
services in market $i$.

The \emph{affordability-driven} component is driven by the fact that
an incremental increase in $p_{ji,k}(\omega)$ can make variety $\omega$
prohibitively expensive for a fraction of existing consumers in market
$i$. The extent of demand loss due to this channel, depends on $(a)$
variety $\omega$'s \emph{degree of affordability} in market $i$,
$p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i}$, as well as $(b)$ the hazard rate
of the income distribution, $\zeta_{i}$.\footnote{As shown in Appendix \ref{sec: Non-Parametric-Model}, even when $G_{i}(y)$
does not exhibit a constant hazard rate, the propositions that follow
hold as long as $G_{i}(y)$ satisfies the IGFR property. } 

\section{Quality Specialization and Pricing-to-Market}

In this section, I use my theoretical model to outline two alternative
drivers of pricing-to-market (PTM) and international quality specialization
(IQS) in discrete industries. This section, therefore, sheds light
on why (as documented in Section \ref{sec:Suggestive-Evidence}) PTM
and IQS occur more intensively in discrete industries. 

\paragraph*{\emph{Pricing-to-Market (PTM).}}

Using the demand elasticity specified by Equation \ref{eq: Eq epsilon},
we can immediately calculate the optimal monopoly price for each traded
variety. Doing so, implies the following price formulation in continuous
($k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}$) and discrete ($k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}$)
industries:
\[
p_{ji,k}(\varphi)=\begin{cases}
\left(1+1/\theta_{k}\right)c_{ji,k}(\varphi) & \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}\\
c_{ji,k}(\varphi)+\vartheta_{i,k}w_{i} & \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}
\end{cases},
\]
with $1/\vartheta_{i,k}\equiv\frac{\theta_{k}}{\tilde{a}_{i}}+\frac{\zeta_{i}}{e_{k}}$
denoting a market-specific \emph{structural} parameter. The above
equation indicates that (absent non-homothetic preferences) there
is no scope for PTM in continuous industries. In discrete industries,
however, PTM occurs even though preferences are homothetic; as suppliers
charge systematically higher prices in markets where $(a)$ they compete
with higher-priced services; and ($b)$ their product is more affordable
to the average consumer.

These results can perhaps explain why PTM is more pronounced in discrete
industries. In both discrete and continuous industries, PTM may be
driven by non-homothetic preferences. But in discrete industries,
PTM is magnified by $(a)$ cross-national heterogeneity in the price
of non-traded services, and $(ii)$ affordability constraints; both
of which are less relevant in continuous industries.

\paragraph*{\emph{International Quality-Specialization (IQS).}}

To fix ideas, allow me to first define IQS formally from the lens
of the present model. Let $Q_{ji,k}(\varphi)\equiv N_{j,k}(\varphi)q_{ji,k}(\varphi)$
denote aggregate export quantity and suppose $\varphi_{H}$ and $\varphi_{L}$
respectively denote a \emph{high} and a \emph{low}-quality tier in
industry $k$, i.e., $\varphi_{H}>\varphi_{L}$. As a matter of definition,
an increase in country-level characteristic $x$ prompts high-quality-specialization
if and only if
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{j}/x_{\ell}}\left\{ \frac{Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/Q_{\ell i,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)}{Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)/Q_{\ell i,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)}\right\} >0,
\]
for (nearly) all $j$, $\ell$, and $i\in\mathbb{C}$. So, to determine
patterns of IQS based on this definition, we need to derive an expression
for the relative exports of $\varphi_{H}$ to $\varphi_{L}$. Doing
so in Appendix \ref{sec: Deriving-Equation for QS}, yields the following
expression:
\begin{equation}
\frac{Q_{ji,k}(\varphi_{H})/Q_{\ell i,k}(\varphi_{H})}{Q_{ji,k}(\varphi_{L})/Q_{\ell i,k}(\varphi_{L})}\approx\begin{cases}
1 & \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}\\
\frac{N_{j,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/N_{\ell,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)}{N_{j,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)/N_{\ell,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)}\ e^{\left(\tau_{\ell i}w_{\ell}a_{\ell,k}-\tau_{ji}w_{j}a_{j,k}\right)\frac{\vartheta_{i,k}}{w_{i}}} & \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}
\end{cases}.\label{eq: IQS}
\end{equation}
The above expression clearly indicates that there is no scope for
IQS in continuous industries. That is because IQS in these industries
is either cost-driven or taste-driven, both of which have been ruled
out by assumption. By contrast, in the case of discrete industries,
the above expression identifies two alternative drivers of IQS that
are neither cost-driven nor taste-driven. 

The first of these are affordability constraints, which operate (primarily)
through the exponential term in Equation \ref{eq: IQS}. The exponential
terms account for the fact that, due to affordability constraints,
an across-the-board increase in the cost of all varieties supplied
by country $j$ has a disproportionally higher effect on demand for
high-quality (high-cost) varieties. To demonstrate this, we can take
a basic derivative from Equation \ref{eq: IQS} with respect to the
national level cost-shifters, $a_{j,k}$, which implies that:
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial a_{\ell,k}/a_{j,k}}\left\{ \frac{Q_{ji,k}(\varphi_{H})/Q_{\ell i,k}(\varphi_{H})}{Q_{ji,k}(\varphi_{L})/Q_{\ell i,k}(\varphi_{L})}\right\} >0\ \ \ \textrm{if }k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}.
\]
Based on the above expression, countries tend to specialize in higher-quality
varieties in industries where they are more cost-efficient. The intuition
is that affordability constraints are more binding for high-quality
varieties. So, an improvement in cost-efficiency (keeping all else
the same) increases market access disproportionally more for high-quality
varieties. Such a link between within-industry IQS and industry-level
cost efficiency is quite unique and has little precedent in the literature.\footnote{The above result offers a possible micro-foundation for the assumption
underlying \citet{alcala2016specialization} that efficiency or productivity
is quality-biased.}

The second driver of IQS in discrete industries is the \emph{home-market
effect}, which operates through the number of firms in Equation \ref{eq: IQS}.
Unlike standard theories, though, the home-market effect here is not
driven by non-homothetic taste for quality. Instead, it is driven
(primarily) by cross-market differences in $\tilde{p}_{i}$. That
is, a higher price of services increases the home-market demand for
quality, leading to high-quality specialization due to scale economies
in production.\footnote{A higher $\tilde{p}_{i}$ lowers the demand elasticity for discrete
goods, which in turn creates relatively more demand for high-quality
(high-cost) product varieties---see \citet{Fajgelbaum2011,matsuyama2015home,dingel2016determinants}
for a similar argument, but in the case where the home-market effect
is driven by non-homothetic preferences over quality. } To demonstrate this point formally, we can take a simple derivate
from the free-entry condition with respect to $\tilde{p}_{i}$, noting
that $\partial\varepsilon_{ji,k}(\varphi)/\partial\tilde{p}_{i}<0$
for all $j$ and $i$. Doing so, implies the following, provided that
international trade costs are sufficiently high:
\begin{equation}
\frac{\partial}{\partial\tilde{p}_{j}/\tilde{p}_{\ell}}\left\{ \frac{N_{j,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/N_{\ell,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)}{N_{j,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)/N_{\ell,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)}\right\} >0\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{\partial}{\partial\tilde{p}_{j}/\tilde{p}_{\ell}}\left\{ \frac{Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/Q_{\ell i,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)}{Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)/Q_{\ell i,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)}\right\} >0.\label{eq: prop_3 eq3}
\end{equation}
Let me reiterate that the \emph{home-market effect} in itself is not
specific to this model. In fact, \citet{costinot2016more} have already
characterized this result under very general conditions.\footnote{In the present model, the scale elasticity (defined as $\partial\ln Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)/\partial\ln N_{j,k}\left(\varphi\right)$
) is equal to ``\emph{one}.'' So, scale effects are strong enough
to trigger a \emph{strong} home-market effect (see \citet{costinot2016more}).
That is, all else equal, high-wage countries are not only \emph{gross}
exporters of high-quality but also \emph{net} exporters of high-quality
varieties. } What is instead novel, is that the \emph{home-market effect} is not
driven by non-homothetic taste but by cross-country differences in
the price of non-traded services. Along similar lines, affordability
constraints can also trigger IQS through the home-market effect, given
that high-quality varieties are more affordable and, therefore, more-demanded
in high-wage markets. The following proposition summarizes the above
results.
\begin{prop}
\label{prop: prop 1}Absent Ricardian comparative cost advantage and
non-nomothetic preferences: (a) There is no scope for either quality
specialization nor pricing-to-market in continuous industries; but
(b) quality specialization and pricing-to-market can still occur in
discrete industries due to cross-national differences in the price
of non-traded services and affordability constraints.
\end{prop}
