Figure \ref{fig:Numerical-Example} elucidates the above arguments
using a simulated economy that features multiple countries and quality
tiers.\footnote{\label{fn: numerical example}The example involves 5 economies producing/consuming
only discrete varieties in 50 different quality tiers: $\varphi=1,...,50$.
Population size in all countries is normalized to one: $L_{j}=1$,
$\forall j$; but countries differ in their productivity: $a_{j}=1+0.25(j-1)$.
The region with the lowest productivity is labeled the \emph{South}
($s$) and the highest productivity region is labeled the \emph{North}
($n$): $a_{s}/a_{n}=2$. I also assume $c(\varphi)=0.08\varphi$,
$f(\varphi)=\varphi^{0.25}$, $\theta=4$, and $\tau_{ji}=2$ for
all $j\neq i$.} It compares two countries in this simulated economy (namely, North,
$n$, and South, $s$) that differ only in a Hicks-neutral cost shifter,
$a_{s}/a_{n}=2$. The left panel assumes all varieties are universally
affordable and IQS is driven by the combination of scale economies
and cross-national differences in $\tilde{p}_{i}$. The right panel
shuts down scale economies, so that IQS is driven solely by affordability
constraints.

A natural follow-up question to Proposition \ref{prop: prop 1} is
whether the alternative forces that drive PTM and IQS in discrete
industries are empirically distinguishable from cost-driven or taste-driven
IQS and PTM? To answer this question, it is useful to define two \emph{aggregate}
trade statistics that are often used to describe standard theories
of IQS and PTM. The first statistic is the industry-level export \emph{unit
price}, which can be defined as
\[
\bar{p}_{ji,k}\equiv\frac{\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}p_{ji,k}(\varphi)Q_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}Q_{ji,k}(\varphi)}.
\]
The second statistic is the industry-level export quality, which can
be analogously defined as:s
\[
\bar{\varphi}_{ji,k}\equiv\frac{\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}\varphi\ Q_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}Q_{ji,k}(\varphi)}.
\]
As proven in Appendix \ref{subsec: Proof Proposition 2}, combining
the above definition with our prior results on PTM and IQS, yields
the following proposition.\vspace{0.1in}
\begin{prop}
\label{prop: 2}$(i)$ Export unit prices are increasing in the price
of non-traded services in the importing market, but only so in discrete
industries:
\[
\begin{cases}
\frac{\partial\bar{p}_{ji,k}(.)}{\partial\tilde{p}_{i}}=0 & \textrm{\textrm{if }k\ensuremath{\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}}}\\
\frac{\partial\bar{p}_{ji,k}(.)}{\partial\tilde{p}_{i}}>0 & \textrm{\textrm{if }k\ensuremath{\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}}}
\end{cases};
\]
$(ii)$ Export unit prices are increasing in the price of non-traded
services in the exporting market, but only so in discrete industries.
\[
\begin{cases}
\frac{\partial\bar{p}_{ji,k}(.)}{\partial\ln\tilde{p}_{j}}=0 & \textrm{\textrm{if }k\ensuremath{\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}}}\\
\frac{\partial\bar{p}_{ji,k}(.)}{\partial\ln\tilde{p}_{j}}>0 & \textrm{\textrm{if }k\ensuremath{\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}}}
\end{cases};
\]
(iii) Export quality is increasing in a country's industry-level degree
of comparative cost advantage, but only so in discrete industries:
\[
\begin{cases}
\frac{\partial\bar{\varphi}_{ji,k}(.)}{\partial a_{j,k}}=0 & \textrm{\textrm{if }k\ensuremath{\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}}}\\
\frac{\partial\bar{\varphi}_{ji,k}(.)}{\partial a_{j,k}}<0 & \textrm{\textrm{if }k\ensuremath{\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}}}
\end{cases}.
\]
\end{prop}
The above proposition presents a set of comparative static results
indicating that \emph{the price of non-traded services }and \emph{cost-efficiency}
have differential effects on aggregate export price/quality levels
in discrete versus continuous industries. In the following section,
I will use the above proposition to empirically test my theory. Before
doing so, let me note that $\tilde{p_{i}}$, $\tilde{p}_{j}$, $a_{j,k}$
affect the price of exports/imports through both the quality and markup
channels. These two channels are independent, but (in the present
setup) they always reinforce one another's effect on prices. That
being the case, I can just rely on readily observable price data to
test the model's predictions. Encouragingly, as I will show next,
the above predictions are all borne out.

\section{\label{sec:Empirical-Evidence}Testing the Predictions of the Model}

Proposition \ref{prop: 2} will serve as the basis for testing my
theory. In particular, I test $(a)$ if the export unit price, $\bar{p}_{ji,k}$,
is positively related to $\tilde{p}_{i}$, $\tilde{p}_{j}$, and $a_{j,k}$;
and also $(b)$ if these relationships are amplified by \emph{discreteness}.
To conduct my analysis, I merge two different datasets. The first
of which is from the 2011 International Comparison Program (ICP) compiled
by the World Bank Development Data Group.\footnote{The ICP data has been released for years 1970, 1973, 1975, 1980, 1985,
1993, 2005, and 2011. Here, I choose 2011 as the benchmark year for
my analysis.} The ICP data reports national expenditures and PPPs for more than
150 \textquotedblleft Basic Headings\textquotedblright{} categories.
This information allows me to construct the aggregate price of non-traded
services, $\tilde{p}_{i}$ for 182 countries.\footnote{I treat the following basic headings in the ICP as non-tradable: 'Housing',
'Education', 'Health', and 'Restaurants and Hotels'. In the main analysis
'Communication' is not treated as a non-tradable heading, but treating
it as one does not alter any of the results qualitatively. Moreover,
similar \citet{sposi2015trade}, I treat \textquotedblleft Change
in inventories and valuables,\textquotedblright{} as unclassified.} 

I merge the \noun{ICP }data with the\noun{ Comtrade-baci} database,
which is the most comprehensive database on export unit prices. The
\noun{baci} data is compiled by the CEPII based on the United Nations
\noun{Comtrade} database but uses a harmonization methodology to reconcile
mirror flows. This harmonization approach provides a more complete
geographical coverage than if only a single direction of \noun{Comtrade}
statistics were to be used---\citet{gaulier2010baci} describe the
\noun{Baci} approach to harmonization, which involves computing a
weighted average of mirror flows. For the year 2011, the \noun{Comtrade-baci}
database reports physical quantities and values of bilateral trade
flows by 6-digit HS product category, allowing me to construct the
corresponding unit price levels. 

Combining the ICP and the BACI datasets, leaves me with a sample of
bilateral trade statistics for 147 importers and 147 exporters across
5,231 HS6 product categories in the year 2011. For each country in
the sample, \citet{head2010erosion} report matching data for GDP,
distance, and population size. So, altogether, for every \emph{exporting
country $j$$\times$importing country $i$$\times$HS6 industry $k$}
(observation $ji,k$), I can construct a quantity-weighted unit price,
$\bar{p}_{ji,k}$, as well as exporter/importer characteristics such
as total GDP, GDP per capita, geo-distance, $\tilde{p}_{j}$, and
$\tilde{p}_{i}$. To test the prediction $(iii)$ from Proposition
\ref{prop: 2}, I also need data on the degree of industry-level comparative
cost advantage. Unfortunately, the technology parameters, $a_{j,k}$,
are not directly observable. So, as is common in the literature, I
infer them from sales data. To this end, I construct the Balassa index
of revealed comparative advantage for each country $j$ in industry
$k$, as follows:\footnote{The results of my analysis are qualitatively robust to adopting alternative
measures of revealed comparative advantage, such as that proposed
by \citet{proudman2000evolving}.}
\[
\textrm{RCA}_{j,k}=\frac{\sum_{i}X_{ji,k}/\sum_{i}\sum_{g}X_{ji,g}}{\sum_{\ell}\sum_{i}X_{\ell i,k}/\sum_{\ell}\sum_{i}\sum_{g}X_{\ell i,g}}
\]
The above measure provides a theory-consistent proxy for $a_{j,k}$;
since from the lens of the model, a lower $a_{j,k}$ (ceteris paribus)
is associated with a higher $RCA_{j,k}$.

The \noun{Baci }data does not explicitly report the units in which
quantity is measured.\footnote{Unlike the U.S. data which identify the unit in which physical quantity
is measured, the \noun{Baci }data only reports the weight-equivalent
of physical quantity for all observations. } So, I use the U.S. import and export data to identify the discrete
product categories, with $\mathbbm{1}_{k\in\mathbb{K_{\mathcal{D}}}}$
denoting the corresponding discrete product dummy.\footnote{By this classification, discrete goods account for 36\% of global
trade in the BACI dataset.} This approach can classify 90\% of observations in the \noun{Baci}.
Alternatively, to preserve all observations, I can classify a HS6
product category as discrete if it belongs to either the ``Machinery,''
``Electrical \& Optical Equipment,'' or ``Transport Equipment''
sectors. Both approaches deliver qualitatively similar results. 

To test the model, I run the following regression on the final sample
that includes 5,249,424 observations:\footnote{Using a linear regression to test the comparative static results outlined
by Proposition \ref{prop: 2}, requires some clarification. In the
words of \citet{reiss2007structural}, the standard reasoning behind
this choice is that \emph{``When the conditional expectation of y
is nonlinear in x,} s\emph{tatistical theory tells us (under certain
sampling assumptions) that a regression provides a best (minimum expected
squared prediction error) linear approximation to the nonlinear conditional
expectation function.'' }However, as \citet{reiss2007structural}
point out, there are basic caveats associated with using a linear
reduced-form specification to test comparative static results.}
\begin{align}
\hspace{-0.2in}\ln\overline{p}_{ji,k}= & \left(\beta_{1}+\beta_{1}^{\mathcal{D}}\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{k\in\mathbb{K_{\mathcal{D}}}}\right)\ln\tilde{p}_{i}\ +\ \left(\beta_{2}+\beta_{2}^{\mathcal{D}}\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{k\in\mathbb{K_{\mathcal{D}}}}\right)\ln\tilde{p}_{j}\nonumber \\
 & \ +\left(\beta_{3}+\beta_{3}^{\mathcal{D}}\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{k\in\mathbb{K_{\mathcal{D}}}}\right)\ln\textrm{RCA}_{j,k}\ +\ Controls_{ji}+\delta_{k}+\epsilon_{ji,k},\label{eq: Baci Regression}
\end{align}
where $\delta_{k}$ controls for HS6 fixed effects; and $Controls_{ji}$
is composed of additional controls including total GDP, GDP per capita,
and geo-distance. %
\begin{comment}
\begin{align*}
\ln\overline{p}_{ji,k}= & \left(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}\cdot disc\right)RCA_{j,k}+\left(\beta_{3}+\beta_{4}\cdot disc\right)\ln\tilde{p}_{j}+\left(\beta_{5}+\beta_{6}\cdot disc\right)\ln\tilde{p}_{i}\\
+ & \beta_{7}\ln w_{j}+\beta_{8}\ln w_{i}+\beta_{9}\ln Y_{j}+\beta_{10}\ln Y_{i}+\beta_{11}\ln\textrm{Dist}_{ji}+\delta_{k}+\epsilon_{ji,k},
\end{align*}
\end{comment}
{} In addition to the baseline specification, I run the above regression
under alternative specifications, controlling for \emph{exporter,
importer,} and \emph{exporter$\times$importer} fixed effects.\footnote{As in Section \ref{sec:Suggestive-Evidence}, since I am dealing with
grouped data each observation is weighted by trade quantity, which
is a theory-consistent measure of the number of firms grouped into
each observation---refer to Section \ref{sec:Suggestive-Evidence}
for a more elaborate discussion.} 

Based on Proposition \ref{prop: 2}, the estimated coefficients $\beta_{1}^{\mathcal{D}}$,
$\beta_{2}^{\mathcal{D}}$, and $\beta_{3}^{\mathcal{D}}$ should
be positive and statistically significant.\footnote{The estimated coefficients $\beta_{1}$, $\beta_{2}$, and $\beta_{3}$
may be positive given that $\mathbbm{1}_{k\in\mathbb{K_{\mathcal{D}}}}$
does not perfectly identify discrete product categories. More specifically,
an industry where $\mathbbm{1}_{k\in\mathbb{K_{\mathcal{D}}}}=0$
may still contain a small fraction of observations that correspond
to discrete goods. } Encouragingly, the estimation results presented in Table \ref{tab:price-regression}
support theses predictions.

In line with prediction $(i)$ from Proposition \ref{prop: 2}, the
elasticity of export prices with respect to the price of non-traded
services in the destination market is significantly higher in discrete
industries. To provide numbers, consider Column 3 that controls for
exporter$\times$HS6 fixed effects. A 10\% increase in $\tilde{p}_{i}$,
is associated with a 1.53\% increase in the price of exports to market
$i$ in discrete industries. But in continuous industries, the effect
is only 0.06\% and statistically insignificant. To put this number
in perspective, the same estimation indicates that a 10\% increase
in the GDP per capita of country $i$ is associated with an only 1.6\%
increase in the price of exports to that market.\footnote{Adding $\ln\textrm{GDP per capita}_{i}\times\mathbbm{1}_{k\in\mathbb{K_{\mathcal{D}}}}$
as an additional control does not change the sign of the coefficients
reported in Table \ref{tab:price-regression}. However, it increases
the standard errors, which can be indicative of multicollinearity
between $\ln\textrm{GDP per capita}_{i}\times\mathbbm{1}_{k\in\mathbb{K_{\mathcal{D}}}}$
and $\mathbbm{1}_{k\in\mathbb{K_{\mathcal{D}}}}\times\ln\tilde{p}_{i}$.}

Prediction $(ii)$ is also borne out, albeit less decisively. Discreteness
has a positive and statistically significant effect on how export
prices vary with the price of non-traded services in the origin country.
In general, this outcome may be driven by services being used as an
input in production. This channel perhaps explains why $\bar{p}_{ji,k}$
and $\tilde{p}_{j}$ are positively correlated, even in continuous
industries. However, in line with the discrete model's prediction,
this positive correlation is significantly more pronounced in discrete
industries; standing around 0.67 percentage points higher (Table \ref{tab:price-regression},
Column 2). 

Finally, prediction $(iii)$ is also borne out: In discrete industries,
a 10\% increase in the origin country's degree of comparative advantage,$\textrm{RCA}_{j,k}$,
is associated with a 0.77\% increase in export prices. In continuous
industries, by comparison, $\textrm{RCA}_{j,k}$ is associated with
a mere 0.21\% increase in export prices (Table \ref{tab:price-regression},
Column 2).\footnote{That $\textrm{RCA}_{j,k}$ matters in continuous industries may be
driven by two factors. First, industries coded as continuous in my

as it reflects either a comparative \emph{quality} advantage or a
comparative \emph{cost} advantage. In the former case, $\textrm{RCA}_{j,k}$
is positively related to $\overline{p}_{ji,k}$, while in the latter
case it is negatively related to $\overline{p}_{ji,k}$.}%

{}  One caveat here, though, is that I am not testing the model's
predictions \emph{directly} with information on quality and markups.
The above analysis, therefore, cannot rule out the case where $\tilde{p}_{j}$,
$\tilde{p}_{i}$, and $\textrm{RCA}_{j,k}$ have countervailing effects
on export markups and qualities. Instead, loosely speaking, the analysis
can only identify the joint effect of these variables on \emph{quality}$\times$\emph{markup}.
This limitation is, however, hard to overcome as estimates for quality
and markup are difficult to attain at the scale in which my analysis
is conducted. This limitation notwithstanding, the above results plus
those presented in Section \ref{sec:Suggestive-Evidence} corroborate
the assertion that IQS and PTM are magnified by additional forces
in discrete industries. 

\paragraph*{Restricting Sample to Differentiated or Final Goods.}

In the above analysis, discreteness may be accounting for other omitted
product characteristics such as the degree of differentiation or intent
of final use. To address this issue, I reestimate Equation \ref{eq: Baci Regression}
on two restricted samples: First, a sample that only includes differentiated
HS6 products as classified by \citet{Rauch1999}. Second, a sample
that includes only HS6 products that are intended for final consumption,
based on the Broad Economic Categories (BEC) classification.

The results derived from these restricted samples are reported in
Table \ref{tab:price-regression-robust}. They indicate that, even
within differentiated goods, discreteness has a significant effect
on how export prices, $\bar{p}_{ji,k},$ vary with the price of services
in the origin and destination economies, $\tilde{p}_{j}$, and $\tilde{p}_{i}$.
Likewise, discreteness has a significant effect on how export prices
vary with the origin country's degree of comparative advantage as
measured by $\textrm{RCA}_{j,k}$. The same applies when we restrict
attention to only final consumption goods. Appendix \ref{sec:Additional-Test-the}
presents an additional test in which HS6 products are grouped into
\emph{more-} or \emph{less-differentiated} bins according to the demand
elasticity estimates in \citet{Broda2006}. Estimating Equation \ref{eq: Baci Regression}
separately for these product groups produces similar results.

\section{\label{sec: GT}The Big Picture: \emph{The Gains from Discrete Trade}}

Does accounting for discrete trade revise our understanding of the
gains from trade? To answer this question, we can appeal to the result
in \citet{McFadden1978} that the expected welfare of each individual
in country $i$ with respect to discrete industry $k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}$
can be expressed as follows:
\[
W_{i,k}\left(y\right)=\exp(y)\left(\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}\left[\varphi\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i,k}\left(y,\varphi\right)}N_{j,k}\left(\varphi\right)\exp\left(p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)\right)^{-\frac{\theta_{k}}{\tilde{p}_{i}}}\right]^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}}\right)^{\frac{1}{\gamma_{k}}},
\]
where $\mathcal{J}_{i,k}\left(y,\varphi\right)=\left\{ j\in\mathbb{C}\mid p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)\leq e_{k}w_{i}y\right\} $
denotes the set of countries from which an individual with endowment
$y$ can affordably buy quality $\varphi$ varieties. Correspondingly,
the expected welfare of the same individual under \emph{autarky }(denoted
by $\textrm{A}$) is given by
\[
W_{i,k}^{\textrm{A}}\left(y\right)=\exp(y)\left(\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}\left(y\right)}\left[\varphi N_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right)\exp\left(p_{ii,k}\left(\varphi\right)\right)^{-\frac{\theta_{k}}{\tilde{p}_{i}}}\right]^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}},\ \ \ k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}
\]
where $\varPhi_{k}\left(y\right)=\left\{ \varphi\in\varPhi_{k}\mid p_{ii,k}\left(\varphi\right)\leq e_{k}w_{i}y\right\} $
denotes the set of quality levels that can be affordably purchased
from domestic suppliers. Combining the above two equations; using
the exact hat-algebra notation, $\hat{x}\equiv x/x^{\textrm{A}}$;
and noting that the gains from trade in \emph{continuous} industries
are governed by the \citet{Arkolakis} (ACR) formula, yields the following
proposition.%
\begin{comment}
\[
\frac{W_{i,k}^{A}\left(y\right)}{W_{i,k}\left(y\right)}=\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}\frac{\left[f_{k}\left(\varphi\right)N_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right)v_{k}\left(y,\tilde{p}_{i},p_{ii,k}\right)\right]^{\gamma_{k}}}{\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}f_{k}\left(\varphi\right)\left[\sum_{j}N_{j,k}\left(\varphi\right)v_{k}\left(y,\tilde{p}_{i},p_{ji,k}\right)^{\theta_{k}}\right]^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}}}
\]

\[
\frac{W_{i}^{A}}{W_{i}}=\frac{\sum_{\varphi}\left(\frac{N_{i,\varphi}^{A}}{N_{i,\varphi}}\lambda_{ii,\varphi}\right)^{\frac{1}{\theta}}f(\varphi)\left(\sum_{k}N_{k,\varphi}h\left(1-\rho_{ki,\varphi}\right)^{\theta}\right)^{\frac{1}{\theta}}}{\sum_{\varphi}f(\varphi)\left(\sum_{k}N_{k,\varphi}h\left(1-\rho_{ki,\varphi}\right)^{\theta}\right)^{\frac{1}{\theta}}}=\sum_{\varphi=1}^{\bar{\varphi}}\left(\frac{\lambda_{ii,\varphi}}{\hat{N}_{i,\varphi}}\right)^{\frac{1}{\theta}}
\]
\[
\frac{\Delta W_{i,k}\left(y\right)}{W_{i,k}(y)}=1-\left(\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}\left[\lambda_{ii,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)^{\frac{1}{\theta_{k}}}/\hat{N}_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right)^{-\frac{1}{\theta_{k}}}\ \widehat{v_{k}\left(y,\tilde{p}_{i},p_{ii,k}\right)}\right]^{\gamma_{k}}\Lambda_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)\right)^{\frac{1}{\gamma_{k}}}
\]
\end{comment}
\vspace{0.1in}
\begin{prop}
\label{prop: GT}{[}\textbf{The Gains from Trade}{]} The gains from
trade\textup{, $GT_{i}\left(y\right)\equiv\Delta W_{i}\left(y\right)/W_{i}(y)$},
for income group $y$ residing in country $i$ are given by
\[
GT_{i}\left(y\right)=1-\prod_{k\in\mathbb{K}}\left(\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}\lambda_{ii,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}}\widehat{N}_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right){}^{-\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}}\ e_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)\right)^{\frac{e_{k}}{\gamma_{k}}},
\]
where $e_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$ denotes the probability of
choosing quality level $\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}$, while $\lambda_{ii,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$
denotes the probability of purchasing a domestic variety.\vspace{0.1in}
\end{prop}
Based on the above proposition, the gains from trade are materialized
through two distinct channels: $(i)$ the \emph{scale-driven }gains
that depend on $\widehat{N}_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right)$; and $(ii)$
the \emph{import variety gains} that depend on $\lambda_{ii,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$.
Beholding this decomposition, let me first qualitatively discuss the
distributional consequences of trade. Then, I will formally quantify
the aggregate gains from discrete trade. 

\paragraph*{\emph{The Distributional Gains from Trade.}}

A straightforward corollary of Proposition \ref{prop: GT} is that
the gains from trade favor consumers that are more likely to purchase
foreign varieties, i.e., consumers who exhibit a low $\lambda_{ii,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$.
In discrete industries, if trade costs are sufficiently large, low-income
individuals cannot afford many imported varieties. Hence, even if
individual-level preferences are homothetic, $\lambda_{ii,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$
can be decreasing in $y$, and the gains from trade can favor high-income
(high-$y$) individuals.

So, how can we reconcile the above claim with the claim in \citet{fajgelbaum2014measuring}
that the gains from trade favor low-income consumers who spend a greater
fraction of their income on tradables? The answer lies in the different
interpretations of $\lambda_{ii,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$ in discrete
versus continuous industries. In continuous industries, $\lambda_{ii,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$
perfectly coincides with the share of expenditure on domestic varieties.
In discrete industries, however, $\lambda_{ii,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$
can be strictly unrelated to the expenditure share. In particular,
high-income individuals may be more likely to purchase imported varieties;
but since they buy only one unit of each good, such a purchase may
exhaust a smaller fraction of their income.%
\begin{comment}
Affordability constraints also have a second-order \emph{pro-competitive}
effect on the gains from trade. Specifically, the additive makeup
charged by domestic firms in market $i$ is equal to $w_{i}\left[\frac{\theta_{k}}{\tilde{a}_{i}}+\frac{\zeta_{i}}{e_{k}}\rho_{ii,k}(\varphi)\right]^{-1}$,
where $\rho_{ii}\left(\varphi\right)$ denotes the importance of the
marginal consumer as measured by purchasing probability, with $\rho_{ii}\left(\varphi\right)\approx1$
to a first-order. The introduction of imported varieties will increase
the weight of the marginal consumers, as they cannot afford some of
the newly-introduced import varieties that come with a high transport
cost tags. As a result domestic firms are encouraged to reduce their
markup to a second-order to accommodate these marginal consumers. 
\end{comment}
{} Quantifying these distributional gains, though, requires detailed
international expenditure data across various income groups. That
type of data is largely inaccessible to researchers at this point.
Given this underlying challenge, I turn my attention instead to quantifying
the aggregate gains from trade.

\paragraph*{\emph{The Aggregate Gains from Trade.}}

My discussion above indicated that affordability constraints matter
for the distributional consequences of trade. Now, I purposely abstract
from these constraints to quantify the representative gains from trade
for the case where affordability constraints are non-binding and preferences
are \emph{Gorman representable}. In this special case, unobservable
quality differentiation is also irrelevant for the aggregate gains
from trade, and we can disregard it hereafter.\footnote{To elaborate, if preferences are \emph{Gorman representable}, then
$\lambda_{ii,k}(y,\varphi)=\lambda_{ii,k}(y,\varphi')$ for all $\varphi$
and $\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}$. Consequently, the quality dimension
disappears from the gains from trade equation in this case. This outcome,
though, is an artifact of assuming that $\theta_{k}$ is uniform across
different quality tiers within the same industry. } The representative gains from trade can, therefore, be expressed
as follows:%
\begin{comment}
{[}Suppose $v_{k}=y/p_{ii,k}^{\alpha}\tilde{p}_{i}^{1-\alpha}$ ,
as $\alpha\rightarrow0$ then why does $N_{i}$ remain relevant? because
the taste matters! so we have to discount the taste parameter!{]} 
\end{comment}
\begin{equation}
GT_{i}=1-\prod_{k\in\mathbb{K}}\left(\lambda_{ii,k}/\hat{N}_{i,k}\right)^{\frac{e_{i,k}}{\theta_{k}}}.\label{eq: GT}
\end{equation}
From the lens of the above formula, \emph{discrete} and \emph{continuous}
industries are distinguished by $(i)$ the different interpretations
of $\lambda_{ii,k}$, and $(ii)$ the different characterizations
of $\hat{N}_{i,k}$ in discrete versus continuous industries. If we
treat all industries as \emph{continuous}, the above formula can be
simply interpreted as the celebrated ACR formula.

\subsection{Computing the Gains From Trade}

To transparently highlight the role of discreteness, I use Equation
\ref{eq: GT} to quantify the gains from trade in two extreme cases.
First, as is common in the literature, I treat the traded sector of
the economy as one integrated \emph{continuous} industry. Second,
I opt for the other extreme, treating the traded sector as one integrated
\emph{discrete} industry. Accordingly, I hereafter drop the industry
subscript, $k$, and use $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ to respectively
indicate if the traded sector is modeled as continuous or as discrete.\footnote{An alternative approach would be to use industry-level data and treat
select industries as discrete. Under this approach the resulting intuitions
would remain qualitatively the same.} 

When applying Equation \ref{eq: GT} under the presumption that the
traded sector is continuous ($k=\mathcal{C}$), $\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{C}}$
can be calculated as the \emph{value }share of domestic goods in tradable
consumption. $\hat{N}_{i,\mathcal{C}}$ can be derived using the free
entry condition. In particular, free entry implies that $N_{i,\mathcal{C}}=r_{i,\mathcal{C}}L_{i}/(1+\theta)f^{e}$,
with $r_{i,\mathcal{C}}$ denoting the share of economy $i$'s total
revenue generated in the traded sector. From this expression we can
conclude that $\hat{N}_{i,\mathcal{C}}=1$ since $r_{i,\mathcal{C}}^{\textrm{A}}=r_{i,\mathcal{C}}=e_{i,\mathcal{C}}$,
where $e_{i,\mathcal{C}}$ denotes the share of expenditure on traded
goods.\footnote{$r_{i,\mathcal{C}}^{\textrm{A}}=r_{i,\mathcal{C}}=e_{i,\mathcal{C}}$
results from assuming one traded sector and balanced trade.} Plugging $\hat{N}_{i,\mathcal{C}}=1$ back in to Equation \ref{eq: GT},
yields the following formula for the gains from trade under the continuous
interpretation of the economy:
\begin{equation}
GT_{i}^{\textrm{ACR}}=1-\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{C}}^{\frac{e_{i,\mathcal{C}}}{\theta}}.\label{eq: GT CES}
\end{equation}
In the other extreme where the traded sector is treated as entirely
discrete ($\mathcal{D}$), $\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{D}}$ can be calculated
as the \emph{quantity }share of domestic goods in tradable consumption.
$\hat{N}_{i,\mathcal{D}}$ can be once again derived from the free
entry condition. As demonstrated in Appendix \ref{subsec: GT Derivation},
free entry implies that $N_{i,\mathcal{D}}=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\left(\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}Y_{\ell}/Y_{i}\right)L_{i}/\theta f^{e}$
and, correspondingly, $N_{i,\mathcal{D}}^{\textrm{A}}=L_{i}/\theta f^{e}$.\footnote{These expressions are derived under the implicit assumption that productivity
in the traded sector is sufficiently high, so that domestic discrete
varieties are affordable to local consumers irrespective of international
trade costs. This assumption ensures that the demand function facing
domestic varieties is continuous and well-defined.} Combining these two expressions, $\hat{N}_{i,\mathcal{D}}=N_{i,\mathcal{D}}/N_{i,\mathcal{D}}^{\textrm{A}}$
is given by
\begin{equation}
\hat{N}_{i,\mathcal{D}}=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}\frac{Y_{\ell}}{Y_{i}}.\label{eq: scale-driven GT}
\end{equation}
Plugging the above expression back into Equation \ref{eq: GT}, yields
the following formula for the gains from trade under the discrete
interpretation of the economy:
\begin{equation}
GT_{i}^{\textrm{Discrete}}=1-\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{D}}^{\frac{e_{i,\mathcal{D}}}{\theta}}\left(\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}Y_{\ell}/Y_{i}\right)^{-\frac{e_{i,\mathcal{D}}}{\theta}},\label{eq: GT one-sector}
\end{equation}
where $e_{i,\mathcal{D}}$ denotes the share of expenditure on categories
where discrete goods are bundled with non-traded services in the consumption
basket.\footnote{See Appendix \ref{tab:List-of-industries} for a descriptive list
of consumption categories that fit this bill.} 

Evaluating Equation \ref{eq: GT CES} is rather straightforward, but
mapping Equation \ref{eq: GT one-sector} to data involves a couple
of auxiliary steps. First, we need to evaluate $\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{D}}$,
which corresponds to the \emph{quantity} share of domestic consumption.
The \noun{Comtrade--baci} database reports import quantities, but
measuring $\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{D}}$ also requires information on
the quantity of domestic consumption. One way to overcome this measurement
challenge is to infer $\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{D}}$ from the domestic
expenditure shares and prices. To demonstrate this, recall that $X_{ji}$
denotes country $i$'s total spending on tradable varieties from country
$j$, with $p_{ji}$ denoting the corresponding price of these varieties.
Given information on $\{X_{ji}\}$ and $\{p_{ji}\}$, we can express
$\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{D}}=Q_{ii}/\sum_{j}Q_{ji}$ as follows
\[
\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{D}}=\frac{X_{ii}/p_{ii}}{X_{ii}/p_{ii}+\sum_{j\neq i}X_{ji}/p_{ji}}=\frac{X_{ii}/X_{i}}{X_{ii}/X_{i}+\left(1-X_{ii}/X_{i}\right)p_{ii}/\overline{p}_{-ii}},
\]
where $X_{i}=\sum_{j}X_{ji}$, while $\overline{p}_{-ii}\equiv\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{X_{ji}}{X_{i}}p_{ji}$
denotes the (trade-weighted average) unit price of country $i$'s
imports from the rest of the world. To evaluate the above equation,
we need data data on $p_{ii}/\overline{p}_{-ii}$ and $\{X_{ji}\}$.
Data on the former variable is obtainable from the Penn World Tables
(PWT), which report aggregate price levels for imports and domestic
expenditure. The data on tradable expenditure values, $\{X_{ji}\}$
are taken from the 2008 version of the World Input-Output Database
(\noun{WIOD}, \citet{timmer2012world}).\footnote{To make the data consistent with theory, I purge it from trade imbalances
following the methodology in \citet{costinot2014trade}. } Combining the aforementioned data, I can measure $\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{D}}$
for 31 countries. Likewise, measures for $e_{i,\mathcal{C}}$ and
$e_{i,\mathcal{D}}$ can be constructed with data on $\{X_{ji}\}$
by grouping industries into traded and non-traded categories---see
Table \ref{tab:List-of-industries} in the appendix for details.\footnote{Table \ref{tab:GT} reports the corresponding values for $e_{i,\mathcal{C}}$
and $e_{i,\mathcal{D}}$ for each of the 31 countries. Unlike the
continuous model that is calibrated to the share of tradable expenditure,
the discrete model is calibrated to $e_{i,\mathcal{D}}$, which is
the sum of expenditure on discrete tradables and matching services.
In Appendix \ref{sec: Construction-of-Figure}, I check if the discrete
model can replicate the (out-of-sample) share of tradable expenditure
in isolation. Reassuringly, the model performs relatively well on
this front.}

The second term in Equation \ref{eq: GT one-sector}, $\left(\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}Y_{\ell}/Y_{i}\right)^{-\frac{e_{i,\mathcal{D}}}{\theta}},$
is computed using bilateral trade quantities, $Q_{j\ell}$, from the
\noun{Comtrade--baci} database described in Section \ref{sec:Empirical-Evidence}.
Specifically, the export quantity share $\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}$
is computed as,
\[
\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}=\frac{Q_{i\ell}}{\sum_{j\neq\ell}Q_{j\ell}}\left(1-\lambda_{\ell\ell,\mathcal{D}}\right).
\]
Data on total domestic absorption, $Y_{i}$, are taken from the PWT.
Plugging values for $\lambda_{\ell i,\mathcal{D}}$ and $Y_{i}$ into
Equation \ref{eq: GT one-sector} and combining it with the previously-constructed
data for $\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{D}}$, allows me to compute the gains
from discrete trade for each of the 31 countries in the 2008 WIOD
sample. For the same set of countries, I can compute the gains implied
by the ACR formula by plugging data values for $e_{i,\mathcal{C}}$,
$e_{i,\mathcal{D}}$, and $\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{C}}=X_{ii}/X_{i}$
into Equation \ref{eq: GT CES}. 

\paragraph*{Estimating $\theta$.}

I estimate $\theta$ using the triple difference approach developed
by \citet{caliendo2014estimates}. This approach is fully described
in Appendix \ref{sec:Estimation-of-theta}, and requires data on bilateral
trade shares and tariff rates. Trade shares are taken directly from
the WIOD. Data on bilateral tariff rates are taken from the United
Nations Statistical Division, Trade Analysis and Information System
(UNCTAD-TRAINS, see Appendix \ref{sec:Estimation-of-theta}). The
estimated $\theta$ is reported in Table \ref{tab:Estimated theta}.
The main difference between the continuous and discrete cases is that
under the former the estimating equation reduces to the familiar log-log
specification implied by CES-based models. Under the latter, the estimating
equation adopts a log-level specification---see Appendix \ref{sec:Estimation-of-theta}
for further details. These differences notwithstanding, both approaches
estimate a relatively similar value for $\theta$, which is in line
with exiting estimates from the literature.\footnote{\citet{Broda2006} estimate an import demand elasticity that is analogous
to $\theta+1$. Their product-level estimates exhibit an average value
of 6.}

\subsection{Quantitative Results}

The computed gains from trade are reported in Table \ref{tab:GT}.
In summary, the discrete interpretation of the data predicts gains
from trade that are on average larger (7.6\% versus $5.9\%$) and
more heterogeneous than those implied by the continuous interpretation.
These differences are driven by two factors: First, from the view
of the discrete model, the gains from trade can be large even if a
country spends a small fraction of its income on tradable goods. To
elaborate, consider the US and Mexican economies that spend a similar
fraction of their income on categories where traded goods are bundled
with services. The US economy, though, spends only 27\% of its total
expenditure on \emph{specifically} traded goods compared to 44\% in
Mexico. The continuous interpretation of the economy attributes this
pattern to the US consumers assigning a lower weight to traded goods
in their preferences. This interpretation inevitably predicts relatively
small gains for the US. The discrete model, however, attributes the
same pattern to the income-inelastic nature of discrete goods and
the higher purchasing power of US consumers relative to Mexican Consumers. 

Second, the discrete model admits \emph{scale-driven} gains that are
highly heterogeneous across countries. They favor small countries
(e.g., Belgium and Canada) or low-income countries (e.g., Brazil and
Indonesia) that are located in the proximity of larger and richer
markets . For instance, the ACR formula predicts that trade increases
Brazil's real GDP by only 1.8\%. The discrete model, meanwhile, predicts
gains of around 6.3\% for Brazil, of which 3.6\% is purely scale-driven.
For Canada, the ACR formula predicts gains of around 5.4\%. The discrete
model predicts 15\% in gains, of which 5.6\% is scale-driven. As I
will elaborate below, these gains are driven by firm-relocation into
these countries from larger and richer trading partners like the US.
Correspondingly, the scale-driven gains from trade are negative for
the US and stand around $-3\%$.

\subsection{Elucidating the Scale-Driven Gains from Discrete Trade }

The scale-driven gains from discrete trade operate through a unique
channel that is akin to a \emph{reverse home-market effect}. After
opening to trade, firms relocate from richer and larger economies
that host their main costumer-base to lower-income countries. Doings
so exposes them to higher trade costs but allows them to collect a
higher markup over marginal cost. To better understand these effects,
consider a world economy with two countries: $i=1,2$. Suppose the
two countries have identical productivity levels and face similar
trade costs, but differ in their population sizes:
\[
a_{1,\mathcal{D}}=a_{2,\mathcal{D}}=a;\ \ \ \ \tilde{a}_{1}=\tilde{a}_{2}=1;\ \ \ \ \tau_{12}=\tau_{21}=\tau>1;\ \ \ \ L_{2}>L_{1}.
\]
In this basic setup, the free entry condition implies that (see Appendix
\ref{subsec: GT Derivation})
\[
N_{i,\mathcal{D}}=\sum_{\ell=1,2}\left(\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}\frac{w_{\ell}L_{\ell}}{w_{i}L_{i}}\right)\frac{L_{i}}{\theta f^{e}},\ \ \ \ i=1,2.\ \ \ \ (\textrm{Free Entry})
\]
Moreover, given that $p_{ij,\mathcal{D}}=\tau aw_{i}+w_{j}/\theta$,
the balanced trade condition can be expressed as follows:
\[
\left(\tau a\frac{w_{2}}{w_{1}}+\frac{1}{\theta}\right)\lambda_{21,\mathcal{D}}w_{1}L_{1}=\left(\tau a\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}+\frac{1}{\theta}\right)\lambda_{12,\mathcal{D}}w_{2}L_{2}.\ \ \ \ \ (\textrm{Balanced Trade})
\]
Combining the balanced trade and free entry conditions yields the
following expression for the number of firm located in country $i=1,2$
(see Appendix \ref{subsec: Equation 17}):
\begin{equation}
N_{i,\mathcal{D}}=\left(1+\frac{\frac{w_{-i}}{w_{i}}-\frac{w_{i}}{w_{-i}}}{\frac{w_{i}}{w_{-i}}+\frac{1}{a\tau\theta}}\lambda_{-ii,\mathcal{D}}\right)\frac{L_{i}}{\theta f^{e}}.\label{eq: N_i,D}
\end{equation}
Since $N_{i}^{\text{A}}=L_{i}/\theta f^{e}$ denotes the mass of firms
under autarky, the above equation states that opening to trade preserves
the total number of firms, globally; but induces firm-relocation from
the high- to low-wage country. The intuition is that by relocating
to the low-wage country, firms can collect a higher multiplicative
markup over marginal cost, as is evident from the optimal price equation,
$p_{ij,\mathcal{D}}=a\tau w_{i}(1+\frac{1}{a\tau\theta}\frac{w_{j}}{w_{i}})$.\footnote{We can see the same effect by reformulating Equation \ref{eq: scale-driven GT}
as follows:
\[
\hat{N}_{i,\mathcal{D}}=\frac{\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\left(1-\mu_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}^{-1}\right)\omega_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}}{\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\left(1-\mu_{\ell i,\mathcal{D}}^{-1}\right)\lambda_{\ell i,\mathcal{D}}},
\]
where $\mu_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}\equiv p_{ji,\mathcal{D}}/c_{ji,\mathcal{D}}$
denotes the multiplicative markup over marginal cost, and $\omega_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}$
denotes the share of market $\ell$ in country $i$'s total exports
($\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\omega_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}=1$). } Furthermore, we can invoke the balanced trade condition to show that
the larger economy, in our example, pays a higher wage, i.e., $w_{2}>w_{1}$.
In that case, Equation \ref{eq: N_i,D} implies that opening to trade
induces firm-relocation from the larger to the smaller country:
\[
\hat{N}_{1,\mathcal{D}}>1;\ \ \ \ \hat{N}_{2,\mathcal{D}}<1.
\]
These effects resemble the \emph{``big-push''} effects of economic
development, as formalized by \citet{rosenstein1943problems}, \citet{lewis1954economic},
and \citet{murphy1989industrialization}. To outline this connection,
note that the scale of production in small or poor economies is constrained
by their inadequate local demand. Opening to trade, however, relocates
production activity towards these economies. In doing so, it provides
them with the necessary pig-push platform to expand.

\section{Concluding Remarks}

\emph{``Why nations trade''} and \emph{``how much they gain from
trade''} are perhaps two of the most central questions in the history
of economic thought. Economists have historically approached these
two questions with trade models that treat all goods as infinitely
divisible. This paper asked how our answers to these old questions
are revised if we account for the discrete nature of traded goods.
In this process, I identified two new drivers of international specialization
and pricing-to-market. I further demonstrated that these previously-overlooked
forces are empirically significant. Perhaps most importantly, I illustrated
that accounting for the discrete or lumpy nature of trade can greatly
modify our estimates for the gains from trade.

In the quest to understand discrete trade, this paper only scratched
the surface. Given the fruitful nature of this preliminary step, several
extensions of the discrete model are in order. First, the model provides
a new perspective on the determinants of market power. In that regard,
it can potentially shed light on the documented rise of global market
power in import-competing industries (see \citeauthor{de2017rise}).
Relatedly, the discrete model can provide a fresh perspective on the
trade slowdown and zeros. To elaborate on the latter subject, there
is a withstanding puzzle as to why the incidence of zero trade is
related to income per capita. Appealing to affordability constraints
can perhaps help resolve this puzzle. Finally, in the interest of
space, the present paper resorted to quantifying the aggregate gains
from discrete trade. Applying the discrete trade framework to micro-level
expenditure data presents a promising avenue for feature research
on the distributional consequences of trade.

\section{\label{sec:The-Firm-Level-Colombian}The Firm-Level Colombian Export
and Import Data}

The firm-level data used in Section \ref{sec:Suggestive-Evidence}
covers the universe of Colombian import and export transactions for
the 2007--2013 period. The data has been collected and made available
by the National Tax Agency. For each import transaction, it identifies
the exporting and importing firm's id, the 10-digit Harmonized System
(HS10) classification to which the imported or exported goods belong,
as well as the f.o.b. value in US dollars, quantity, and the unit
in which quantity is reported. 

The import database features 7,296 distinct HS10 product categories,
and 226,288 firms from 251 different countries. Each of these import
transactions is conducted by Colombian firm that is identified by
their unique 9-digits tax id. In total there are 95,071 of such importers,
most of which import a wide range of discrete and non-discrete HS10
products. The export database features 6,590 distinct HS10 product
categories sold to 231 different markets. Each of these export transactions
is conducted by Colombian firm that is identified by their unique
9-digits tax id. In total there are 33,075 exporting firms in the
database, many of which export a wide range of discrete and non-discrete
HS10 products to various markets.

\begin{onehalfspace}
The Colombia import and export data report quantity in 10 different
units. The vast majority of entries report quantity either in counts,
\emph{``UNIDADES O ARTICULOS''}, or in kilograms, \emph{``KILOGRAMO.''}
72\% of all observations in the import data (51\% in value terms)
involve goods that report quantity in counts. In comparison, 63\%
of all observations in the export data (12\% in value terms) involve
goods that report quantity in counts. I classify such goods are \emph{discrete}
and classify all other goods as \emph{continuous}.
\end{onehalfspace}

\section{\label{sec: Non-Parametric-Model}Non-Parametric Model}

In this appendix, I present a general non-parametric version of the
model, which features the following elements: $(i)$ the demand-side
is governed by a general non-parametric discrete choice framework
that can reproduce an important class of continuous and discrete demand
functions, $(ii)$ income heterogeneity is governed by a non-parametric
endowment distribution, $G_{i}(y)$, and $(iii)$ the supply-side
is identical to the baseline model.

\subsection*{General Discrete Choice Preference Structure }

Demand in all industries is characterized by a general discrete choice
framework that can reproduce an important class of well-known demand
systems. As in the baseline model, the economy is populated with $k=1,...,K$
industries, with $e_{k}$ denoting the constant share of expenditure
on industry $k$. Unless stated otherwise, the notation is similar
to the one used in Section \ref{sec:Theoretical-Framework}. The utility
individual $\iota$ extracts from choosing variety $\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)$
and consuming $q_{ji,k}(\omega)$ units of it plus $\tilde{q}$ hours
of industry $k$-related services is given by:
\[
U_{\iota}(q(\omega),\tilde{q};\varphi)=\mathcal{U}_{k}(\tilde{q},q(\omega);\varphi)\ +\ \xi_{\iota}(\omega),\ \ \ \omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi,y)
\]
where $\xi_{\iota}(\omega)$ is an \emph{individual$\times$variety}-specific
utility shifter that accounts for individual $\iota$'s personal taste
for variety $\omega$. $\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi,y)\subset\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)$
denotes the subset of varieties affordable to an individual with endowment
$y$. An individual residing in country $i$ with endowed $y_{\iota}$
has a budget equal to $e_{k}y_{\iota}w_{i}$. The discrete choice
problem facing them, therefore, can be stated as
\begin{align*}
\max_{q(\omega),\tilde{q}}\ \ \  & \mathcal{U}_{k}(\tilde{q},q(\omega);\varphi)+\xi_{\iota}(\omega)\\
\textrm{s.t.}\ \ \  & \tilde{p}_{i,k}\ \tilde{q}+p_{ji,k}(\omega)\ q(\omega)\leq e_{k}y_{\iota}w_{i}\ .
\end{align*}
 The above problem can be solved in two separate steps. First, conditional
on choice $\omega$, the optimal choice for $q(\omega)$ and $\tilde{q}$
can be attained by maximizing $\mathcal{U}_{k}(.)$ subject to the
budget constraint. This stage delivers an indirect utility function
$V_{k}\left(yw_{i},\tilde{p}_{i,k},p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)$, which
can be used to solve the second stage, which is choosing the optimal
variety $\omega$ given the menu of prices and individual taste. Namely,
\begin{equation}
\max_{\omega}\ \ \ V_{k}\left(yw_{i},\tilde{p}_{i,k},p_{ji,k}(\omega);\varphi\right)\ +\ \xi_{\iota}(\omega).\label{eq: indirect utility}
\end{equation}
To simplify the notation, I define $\mathcal{V}_{k}\left(.\right)\equiv\exp(V_{k}(.))$.
Moreover, to decouple the role of \emph{horizontal} and \emph{vertical}
differentiations, I assume that $\mathcal{V}_{k}(.)$ is separable
in quality:
\[
\mathcal{V}_{k}\left(yw_{i},\tilde{p}_{i,k},p_{ji,k}(\omega);\varphi\right)=v_{k}\left(yw_{i},\tilde{p}_{i,k},p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)\ f_{k}(\varphi)
\]
As in the baseline model, $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\iota,k}\equiv\left\{ \xi_{\iota}(\omega)\right\} $
is drawn independently from a General Extreme Value distribution,
$F_{k}(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{k})=\exp\left(-\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}\left(\sum_{\omega}\exp(\xi(\omega))^{-\theta_{k}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}/\theta_{k}}\right)$,
where $\theta_{k}\geq\gamma_{k}\geq0$. With this assumption, we can
invoke the theorem of \emph{General Extreme Value} (\citet{McFadden1978,ben1985discrete})
to produce the following lemma about \emph{individual-level} and \emph{market-level}
demand functions.\footnote{Proof provided in Appendix \ref{sec:Proof-of-Lemma 1}.} 
\begin{lem}
The probability of choosing variety $\omega\in\Omega_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$
by an individual with is
\[
\lambda_{k}\left(y,w_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\tilde{p}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{P}_{i}(y)\right)=\mathcal{V}_{k}\left(yw_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega),\widetilde{p}_{i,k};\varphi\right)^{\theta_{k}}\ \frac{P_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)^{\theta_{k}-\gamma_{k}}}{\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}P_{i,k}\left(\varphi',y\right)^{-\gamma_{k}}},
\]
where $P_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)\equiv\left[\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)}\mathcal{V}_{k}\left(yw_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega),\widetilde{p}_{i,k};\varphi\right)^{\theta_{k}}\right]^{\frac{-1}{\theta_{k}}}$is
an income- and quality-specific demand shifter. Accordingly, the market-level
Marshallian demand facing variety $\omega\in\Omega_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$
can be expressed as\footnote{In order to make the notation more compact, I use $\boldsymbol{P}_{i}(y)$
instead $\boldsymbol{P}_{i}(yw_{i})$.}
\[
\hspace{-0.25in}q_{k}\left(w_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\tilde{p}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)=\left[\int_{y}\mathcal{D}_{k}\left(yw_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\tilde{p}_{i,k}\right)\lambda_{k}\left(y,p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\tilde{p}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{P}_{i}(y)\right)dG_{i}\left(y\right)\right]L_{i},
\]
where $\mathcal{D}_{k}\left(.\right)$ is the demand function associated
with $V_{k}\left(.\right)$.
\end{lem}
In the above lemma, $\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}(y)=\left\{ P_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)\right\} $
and $\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}=\left\{ \boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}(y)\right\} $
denote the vector of demand shifters for various quality levels and
income groups. Likewise, I use $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{i,k}\left(y\right)\equiv\left\{ \Omega_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)\right\} _{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}$
to denote the complete set of varieties (from all quality levels)
affordable to individuals with endowment $y$ in market $i$. 

At this point, it is useful to formally define homothetic preferences
from the lens of the model. I say that individual-level preferences
are homothetic iff
\[
\partial\lambda_{k}\left(y,w_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\tilde{p}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{P}_{i}(y)\right)/\partial y=0,
\]
provided that $\partial$$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{i,k}\left(y\right)/\partial y=0$.
The above definition outlines two sources of income-driven variation
in individual-level demand. First, conditional on choosing from the
same set of affordable varieties, $\lambda_{k}\left(.\right)$ may
vary with $y$ due to the functional-form of the indirect utility
function, $\mathcal{V}_{k}\left(.\right)$. Second, $\lambda_{k}\left(.\right)$
may vary with $y$ due to the expansion of set $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{i,k}\left(y\right)$
with $y$.\footnote{Following the chain rule, if $\lambda_{k}(.)$ is invariant to income,
so is the individual-level demand elasticity, $\epsilon_{k}\left(.\right)\equiv\partial\ln\lambda_{k}\left(.\right)/\partial\ln p_{ji,k}(\omega)$.
Likewise, if preferences are homothetic (as defined above) the share
of individuals that chose a variety with quality $\varphi$, namely,
$\Lambda_{i,k}\left(y,\varphi\right)\equiv P_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)^{-\gamma_{k}}/\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}P_{i,k}\left(\varphi',y\right)^{-\gamma_{k}}$,
does not vary with $y$. } In what follows, I apply the demand system characterized by Lemma
1 to two special cases: $(i)$ continuous industries, and $(ii)$
discrete industries. 

\subsubsection*{(a) Continuous Industries}

Continuous industries involve goods that are $(i)$ infinitely divisible,
and $(ii)$ not directly substitutable with services. As a result,
all continuous goods are affordable to all individuals by assumption,
i.e., $\Omega_{i,k}(\varphi,y)=\Omega_{i,k}(\varphi)$ for all $y$.
I implement these features in my general discrete choice model by
assuming that individuals spend their entire budget on buying multiple
units of their preferred variety: $q(\omega)=e_{k}yw_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)$.
As we will see shortly, at the market-level, this choice structure
is isomorphic to individuals having \emph{indirectly} additive preferences
and buying a fractional quantity of multiple varieties. The indirect
utility, therefore, can be formulated as\footnote{To be clear, the price of non-traded services does not enter the indirect
utility function, because of the implicit assumption that continuous
goods are not directly substitutable with services.}
\[
\mathcal{V}_{k}\left(.\right)=v_{k}\left(e_{k}yw_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)\ f_{k}\left(\varphi\right),\ \ \ \omega\in\Omega_{k}\left(\varphi\right).
\]
Plugging the above characterization of $\mathcal{V}_{k}\left(.\right)$
into Lemma 1, the probability that a consumer with income $y$ in
country $i$ chooses variety $\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(\varphi\right)$
is given by
\[
\lambda_{k}\left(y,e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}(y)\right)=v_{k}\left(ye_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)^{\theta_{k}}\ \frac{P_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)^{\theta_{k}-\gamma_{k}}}{\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}P_{i,k}\left(\varphi',y\right)^{-\gamma_{k}}},
\]
where $P_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)=f_{k}\left(\varphi\right)\left[\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(\varphi\right)}v_{k}\left(ye_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)^{\theta_{k}}\right]^{\frac{-1}{\theta_{k}}}$.
Another characteristic of continuous industries is that all varieties
are accessible to all consumers---i.e., $\Omega_{i,k}\left(y,\varphi\right)=\Omega_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right)$
for all $y$. Correspondingly, the market-level demand facing firm
$\omega$ in market $i$ can be calculated as
\begin{equation}
q_{k}\left(e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)=\left[\int_{y}\left(ye_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)\lambda_{k}\left(y,e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}(y)\right)dG_{i}\left(y\right)\right]L_{i},\label{eq: cont. demand}
\end{equation}
where the above expression uses the fact that $\mathcal{D}_{k}\left(.\right)\equiv ye_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)$.
The above demand function is identical to that arising from indirectly
additive preferences.\footnote{See \citet{bertoletti2018international} for an elaborate review of
indirectly additive preferences.} This class of preferences includes the CES demand system presented
in Section \ref{sec:Theoretical-Framework} as a special case, where
$v_{k}(x)=x$. The above demand function immediately characterizes
the market-level price elasticity of demand, both in the general case
and in the special case where preferences are homothetic (i.e., CES).
\begin{lem}
{[}\textbf{Demand Elasticity in Continuous Industries}{]}\\
$(a)$ The market-level Marshallian demand elasticity facing firm
$\omega\in\Omega_{i,k}(\varphi)$ depends primarily on the average
consumption level in market $i$ (i.e., $e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)$):
\[
\varepsilon_{ji,k}(\omega)=\varepsilon_{k}\left(e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi;\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)\ \ \ ,k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}.
\]
$(b)$ In the case where preferences are homothetic (i.e., $\mbox{x\ensuremath{v_{k}}'\ensuremath{\left(x\right)}/\ensuremath{v_{k}\left(x\right)}=1}$),
the market-level Marshallian demand elasticity is constant: $\varepsilon_{ji,k}(\omega)=1+\theta_{k}$.\footnote{More generally, individual-level preferences are invariant to income
if $xv_{k}'\left(x\right)/v_{k}\left(x\right)=constant_{k}$; but
here to simplify the exposition focus on the case where $xv_{k}'\left(x\right)/v_{k}\left(x\right)=1$.}
\end{lem}
A formal proof for the above lemma is provided in Appendix \ref{sec:Proof-Lemma2}.
But the basic intuition behind Lemma 2 can be provided by focusing
on the case without income heterogeneity. In this special case, the
market-level demand elasticity is given by 
\[
\varepsilon_{k}\left(\bar{q}_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi\right)=1+\theta_{k}\frac{\bar{q}_{ji,k}(\omega)\ v_{k}'\left(\bar{q}_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)}{v_{k}\left(\bar{q}_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)}.
\]
where $\bar{q}_{ji,k}(\omega)\equiv e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)$.
The above formula implies that the main source of variation in the
market-level demand elasticity is the level of consumption. Moreover,
$\varepsilon_{k}\left(.\right)$ is strictly increasing in the average
consumption level, $\bar{q}$, as long as individual-level demand
satisfies the sub-convexity assumption, $\frac{\partial}{\partial q}\frac{qv'_{k}\left(q\right)}{v_{k}\left(q\right)}<0$,
which is also known as Marshall's second law of demand (\citet{mrazova2017not}).
The above property is at the core of many existing theories of PTM
and IQS. That is, as individuals become richer and consume more, they
become less price-sensitive. Correspondingly, firms charge higher
markups in markets that are populated with high-income, less price-sensitive
individuals. The special case where preferences are homothetic (i.e.,
$qv_{k}'\left(q\right)/v_{k}\left(q\right)=1$), is isomorphic to
the CES model. The fact that the homotheticity and constant elasticity
of market-level demand coincide, is a basic corollary of Bergson\textquoteright s
theorem. This result is significant, as it states that the market-level
demand for continuous goods varies across low- and high-wage markets
only and only if individual-level preferences are non-homothetic.\footnote{There is another well-known class of continuous demand functions,
popularized by \citet{arkolakiselusive} (ACDR), where the market-level
demand elasticity varies not directly as a function of individual
consumption, but as function of price $p_{ji,k}(\omega)$ relative
to a market-level choke price. The ACDR class of preferences is closely
related to the indirectly additive preferences nested by the present
model. However, to formally reproduce the ACRD class of demand systems
with a discrete choice framework, one has to impose stronger functional
form assumptions on $\mathcal{V}_{k}\left(.\right)$---see \citet{thisse2016can}
who reproduce the ACDR demand system using a multinomial logit framework.}

\subsubsection*{(b) Discrete Industries}

Discrete industries involve goods that are $(i)$ indivisible, and
$(ii)$ substitutable with services. I implement these features in
my general discrete choice model by assuming that individuals acquire
\emph{one} unit of their preferred discrete variety, and spend the
rest of their budget on corresponding services. They can also forgo
paying an acquisition cost by spending their entire budget on services.\footnote{Theoretically, the choice of forgoing a discrete purchase can be thought
of as follows. There is a choice category $\tilde{\varphi}\in\varPhi_{k}$
(in addition to all existing categories), which consists of homogeneous
varieties (i.e., $\tilde{\theta}\rightarrow\infty$ in this particular
category). Each variety pertaining to this category is priced competitively
at $\tilde{p}_{i,k}$. Hence, choosing a variety from this category
is akin to spending one's entire budget on services.} Considering this, an individual with endowment $y$ who opts for
variety, $\omega\in\Omega_{k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$, purchases one
unit (i.e., $q(\omega)=1$) and is left with $e_{k}yw_{i}-p_{ji,k}(\omega)$
to spare on services. The indirect utility associated with $\mathcal{U}_{k}(.)$
can, therefore, be expressed as
\[
\mathcal{V}_{k}\left(.\right)=v_{k}\left([e_{k}w_{i}y-p_{ji,k}(\omega)]/\tilde{p}_{i,k}\right)\ f_{k}\left(\varphi\right),\ \ \ \omega\in\Omega_{i,k}\left(y,\varphi\right)
\]
Plugging the above formulation into Lemma 1, implies that the individual-level
probability of choosing variety $\omega\in\Omega_{i,k}\left(y,\varphi\right)$
is given by
\begin{equation}
\lambda_{k}\left(y,p_{ji,k}(\omega)/\tilde{p}_{i,k},\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\left(y\right)\right)=v_{k}\left(\tilde{e}_{i,k}y-\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}}\right)^{\theta_{k}}\frac{P_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)^{\theta_{k}-\gamma_{k}}}{\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}P_{i,k}\left(\varphi',y\right)^{-\gamma_{k}}},\label{eq: Demand}
\end{equation}
where $\tilde{e}_{i,k}\equiv e_{k}/\tilde{a}_{i,k}$, and $P_{i}\left(\varphi,y\right)=f_{k}\left(\varphi\right)\left[\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{j,k}(y,\varphi)}v_{k}\left(\tilde{e}_{i,k}y-p_{ji,k}(\omega)/\tilde{p}_{i,k}\right)^{\theta_{k}}\right]^{\frac{1}{\theta_{k}}}$.
Noting that $\mathcal{D}_{k}\left(.\right)=1$, the market-level demand
facing variety $\omega$ can, therefore, be expressed as
\begin{equation}
q_{k}\left(p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega)/\tilde{p}_{i,k},\varphi,\boldsymbol{\text{\ensuremath{P}}}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)=\left[\int_{\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}}}^{\infty}\lambda_{k}\left(y,p_{ji,k}(\omega)/\tilde{p}_{i,k},\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\left(y\right)\right)dG_{i}(y)\right]L_{i}.\label{eq: Demand discrete}
\end{equation}
where, unlike the continuous case, the above aggregation takes into
account that variety $\omega$ is affordable only to consumers with
an endowment $y\geq p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i}$. 

Before moving forward, it should be noted that the above framework
differs from existing discrete choice trade models (e.g., \citet{verhoogen2008trade}
and \citet{Fajgelbaum2011}) in two key aspects. First, the present
setup allows for discrete goods to be combined with ``non-traded''
services, whereas prior discrete choice models do not feature a non-traded
sector.\footnote{To be specific, the present framework can replicate \citet{verhoogen2008trade}
under the following assumptions: $(i)$ $v(x)=e^{\alpha x}$ and $f\left(x\right)=e^{\beta x}$;
$(ii)$ all varieties are affordable; $(iii)$ services are costlessly
traded across markets, i.e., $\tilde{p}_{i}=1$ for all $i$ (\citet{verhoogen2008trade}
though allows $f\left(.\right)$ to be market-specific). Likewise,
the present framework can replicate the framework in \citet{Fajgelbaum2011}
under the following assumptions: $(i)$ $V\left(y,\tilde{p}_{i},p_{\omega i},\varphi\right)=\exp\left(\varphi\left(y-p_{\omega i}\right)/\tilde{p}_{i}\right)$,
$(ii)$ all varieties are affordable, and $(iii)$ services are costlessly
traded across markets, i.e., $\tilde{p}_{i}=1$ for all $i$. Note,
however, that the framework in \citet{Fajgelbaum2011} does not satisfy
Assumption A1, which as stated earlier is not consequential to any
of our claims that follow.} Second, the present model allows for affordability constraints to
bind. Using Equation \ref{eq: Demand discrete}, I can derive the
market-level demand elasticity both in the general case and in the
homothetic case.
\begin{lem}
{[}\textbf{ Demand Elasticity in Discrete Industries}{]}\\
$(a)$ The market-level Marshallian demand elasticity facing firm
$\omega\in\Omega_{i,k}(\varphi)$ is primarily a function of its overall
affordability (i.e., $p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i}$) and its price
relative to non-traded services (i.e., $p_{ji,k}(\omega)/\tilde{p}_{i,k}$)
:%
\begin{comment}
\begin{align*}
\varepsilon\left(p_{\omega}/w_{i},\varphi\right)= & \frac{p_{\omega}}{w_{i}}\frac{\lambda\left(p_{\omega}/w_{i};\varphi\right)}{\lambda\left(\bar{\chi};\varphi\right)}\frac{g_{i}\left(p_{\omega}/w_{i}\right)}{1-G_{i}\left(p_{\omega}/w_{i}\right)}\\
+ & \frac{\theta\frac{p_{\omega}}{w_{i}}\left(\int_{\frac{p_{\omega}}{w_{i}}}^{\infty}\frac{h'\left(\chi-\frac{p_{\omega}}{w_{i}}\right)}{h\left(\chi-\frac{p_{\omega}}{w_{i}}\right)}\lambda\left(p_{\omega}/w_{i},\omega\right)dG_{i}(\chi)\right)}{\int_{\frac{p_{\omega}}{w_{i}}}^{\infty}\lambda\left(p_{\omega}/w_{i},\omega\right)dG_{i}(\chi)}
\end{align*}
\end{comment}
\[
\varepsilon_{ji,k}(\omega)=\varepsilon_{k}\left(p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega)/\tilde{p}_{i,k},\varphi;\boldsymbol{P}_{i},G_{i}\right),\ \ \ k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}.
\]
$(b)$ In the case where preferences are homothetic (i.e., $v_{k}'\left(x\right)/v_{k}\left(x\right)=1)$,
the market-level demand elasticity is given by 
\[
\varepsilon_{ji,k}(\omega)=\theta_{k}p_{ji,k}(\omega)/\tilde{p}_{i,k}+\rho_{ji,k}(\omega)\mathcal{H}_{i}(p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i})p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i},\ \ \ k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}.
\]
where $\rho_{ji,k}(\omega)$ reflects the importance of the marginal
consumers and $\mathcal{H}_{i}\left(.\right)$ denotes the hazard
rate of the income distribution in market $i$.
\end{lem}
The above lemma, which is proven in Appendix \ref{sec: Proof-Lemma3},
indicates that one source of cross-market variation in $\varepsilon_{k}\left(.\right)$
is the functional-form of $v_{k}\left(.\right)$. Specifically, if
$v_{k}'\left(x\right)/v_{k}\left(x\right)\neq1$, preferences will
be non-homothetic and will naturally produce cross-market heterogeneity
in demand. The demand elasticity corresponding to the homothetic case
differs from the formula presented in Section \ref{sec:Theoretical-Framework},
because it is derived under an arbitrary endowment distribution, $G_{i}(y)$.
The empirically-relevant case, though, is one where the income distribution
satisfies the IGFR property.\footnote{IGFR stands for Increasing Generalized Failure Rate, which is satisfied
by nearly all empirically-relevant income distributions (see \citet{lariviere2001selling}
and \citet{lariviere2006note}).} In that case, $\mathcal{H}_{i}(x)x$ is increasing and $\varepsilon_{ji,k}(\omega)$
is lower the more the affordable variety $\omega$. The term $\rho_{ji,k}(\omega)$,
is the purchase probability of variety $\omega$'s marginal consumers
relative to its average consumer. Theoretically, $\rho_{ji,k}(\omega)$
may be greater than 1, even when preferences are homothetic. That
is because the marginal consumer buying $\omega$ may be choosing
from a narrower set of affordable varieties. However, for any variety
$\omega$, we can set $\rho_{ji,k}(p_{ji,k}(\omega))\approx1$ to
a first-order approximation if $(i)$ $v'_{k}\left(.\right)/v_{k}\left(.\right)=1$,
and $(ii)$ $\Omega_{i,k}(\varphi)$ is composed of a discrete set
of varieties.%
\begin{comment}
Lemma 3 outlines two conditions that necessary and sufficient for
homotheticity, which reflects the two distinct drivers of non-homotheticiy
in discrete models. The condition $v'_{k}\left(.\right)/v_{k}\left(.\right)=1$
ensures that conditional on the menu of affordable varieties, the
probability if choosing quality $\varphi$ is independent of income.
However, due to affordability constraints, consumers with different
income levels may have access to a different menu of affordable varieties.
Condition $\gamma_{k}\rightarrow0$ (which is akin to the Cobb-Douglas
assumption), ensures that even then the probability of choosing quality
$\varphi$ is uniform across income levels.
\end{comment}
\begin{comment}
{[}The within-region Engel curve is flatter than the across-region
Engel curve?{]}
\end{comment}


\subsection*{Equilibrium}

Given Lemmas 2 and 3, the demand elasticity facing variety $\omega$
in market $i$ is uniquely determined by $p_{ji,k}(\omega)/w_{i}$
plus market-level demand shifters, $\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}$. The symmetry
of firms within economy $j$ entails that they all charge the same
price $p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)$ for industry $k$ goods as a
function of quality $\varphi$. Defining $\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)\equiv p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)/w_{i}$,
we can express the optimal monopoly pricing equation as follows:\footnote{In the discrete case the existence of a solution is implied by the
fact that $\varepsilon_{k}\left(.\right)$ is increasing in $\nu_{ji,k}(\varphi)$. }
\[
\nu_{ji,k}(\varphi)=\frac{\varepsilon_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}(\varphi),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)}{\varepsilon_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}(\varphi),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)-1}\frac{\tau_{ji}a_{j,k}c(\varphi)w_{j}}{w_{i}},
\]
where $\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}=\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\left(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{N}_{k},\boldsymbol{\nu}_{i,k}\right)$
is uniquely determined by $\boldsymbol{\nu}_{i,k}\equiv\left\{ \nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)\right\} _{\omega\in\Omega_{k}\left(\varphi\right),\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}$,
the vector of aggregate wage rates, $\boldsymbol{w}=\left\{ w_{i}\right\} _{i}$,
and number of firms $\boldsymbol{N}_{k}=\left\{ N_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right)\right\} _{i\in\mathbb{C},\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}$.
Similarly, given $\boldsymbol{\nu}_{i,k}$, $\boldsymbol{w}$, and
$\boldsymbol{N}_{k}$ we can uniquely pin down the matrix of industry-level
bilateral trade values as
\begin{equation}
X_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{N}_{k},\boldsymbol{\nu}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)=\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)N_{j,k}\left(\varphi\right)\bar{\lambda}_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)Y_{i}\label{eq: EQ trade values-1}
\end{equation}
where $\bar{\lambda}_{k}\left(.\right)\equiv q_{k}\left(.\right)/L$
denotes the market-level probability of choosing an imported variety.
Subsequently, given the matrix $\boldsymbol{X}_{k}\equiv\left\{ X_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{N}_{k},\boldsymbol{\nu}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)\right\} _{j,i\in\mathbb{C},\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}$,
we can calculate the variable profits in each country and industry.

So, altogether, we can define the equilibrium as a vector of normalized
prices $\boldsymbol{\nu}_{i,k}$, wage rates $\boldsymbol{w}$, number
of firms $\boldsymbol{N}_{k}$, and market-specific demand shifters,
$\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}=\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\left(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{N}_{k},\boldsymbol{\nu}_{i,k}\right)$,
that satisfy $(i)$ the optimal pricing equation, $(ii)$ the balanced
trade condition (BT), and $(iii)$ the zero-profit condition (FE):
\[
\hspace{-0.25in}\begin{cases}
\nu_{ji,k}(\varphi)=\frac{\varepsilon_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}(\varphi),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)}{\varepsilon_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}(\varphi),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)-1}\frac{\tau_{ji}a_{j,k}c(\varphi)w_{j}}{w_{i}} & \hspace{-0.1in}\forall\varphi\in\varPhi_{k},k\in\mathbb{K}\\
\sum_{j}\sum_{k}\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}X_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{N}_{k},\boldsymbol{\nu}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)=\sum_{\ell\in}\sum_{k}\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}X_{i\ell,k}\left(\varphi,\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{N}_{k},\boldsymbol{\nu}_{i,k},G_{i}\right) & \forall k\in\mathbb{K}\ \ \ (\mathbf{BT})\\
N_{j,k}\left(\varphi\right)=\left\{ \sum_{i}\frac{\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)\ \bar{\lambda}_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}(\varphi),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)}{\varepsilon_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k},G_{i}\right)}\frac{Y_{i}}{Y_{j}}\right\} \frac{L_{j}}{f_{k}^{e}(\varphi)} & \forall k\in\mathbb{K}\ \ \ (\mathbf{FE})
\end{cases},
\]
By Walras' law, the satisfaction of the BT and FE conditions ensures
that labor markets also clear in each country.%

{[}\emph{Note to self}: based on the present theory the price of tradables
increase with $w_{i}$ at a lower elasticity than non-tradables.{]}
