\subsection*{IQS and PTM: \emph{Discrete vs. Continuous Industries}}

Recall that, when preferences are homothetic, the demand elasticity
is $(a)$ constant and uniform across markets in continuous industries,
but $(ii)$ variable and heterogeneous across markets in discrete
industries. This outcome immediately implies that we can produce the
following analog of Proposition \ref{prop: prop 1}, using the general
non-parametric model. 
\begin{prop}
$(a)$ Non-homothetic preferences and Ricardian technology differences
are the only drivers of international quality specialization and pricing-to-market
in continuous industries; but $(b)$ in discrete industries, international
quality specialization and pricing-to-market may be alternatively
driven by affordability constraints and cross-national heterogeneity
in the price of non-traded services.
\end{prop}
The proof of the above theorem follows trivially from Lemmas 2 and
3, but needs a basic qualification. There exist a class of continuous
preferences that are \emph{not} indirectly additive, but are homothetic
and imply a non-constant demand elasticity, e.g., Kimball preferences.
In that case, the above proposition should be restated as follows:
PTM may occur under homothetic preferences, but not PTM as a function
of income per capita, which is the focus of this paper.

\section{Proofs and Derivations}

\subsection{\label{sec:Proof-of-Lemma 1}Demand Shares under General Discrete
Choice Preferences}

Suppose the utility of the individual $\iota$ with income $Y$ can
be expressed as
\[
U_{\iota}(\omega)=\ln V_{k}(Y,p_{ji,k}(\omega),\tilde{p}_{i,k})+\xi_{\iota}(\omega),\ \ \ \omega\in\Omega_{j,k}(\varphi)
\]
In this appendix, I invoke the theorem of ``general extreme value''
to characterize the share of consumers who choose variety $\omega$
as their preferred variety. To this end, define $H_{k}(\boldsymbol{V})$
as follows
\[
H_{k}(\boldsymbol{V})=\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}\left(\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)}A(\varphi)V(\omega)^{\theta_{k}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}/\theta_{k}}
\]
where $\boldsymbol{V}\equiv\{V(\omega)\}$, with $V(\omega)\equiv V_{k}(Y,p_{ji,k}(\omega),\tilde{p}_{i,k})$.
Note that $H_{k}(.)$ is a continuous and differentiable function
of vector $\boldsymbol{V}$ and has the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $H_{k}(.)\geq0$;
\item $H_{k}(.)$ is a homogeneous function of rank $\theta_{k}$: $H_{k}(\rho\boldsymbol{V})=\rho^{\gamma_{k}}H_{k}(\boldsymbol{V})$;
\item $\lim_{V(\omega)\rightarrow\infty}H_{k}(\boldsymbol{V})=\infty,\ \forall\omega\in\cup_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\Omega_{j,k}$;
\item the $m$'th partial derivative of $H_{k}(.)$ with respect to a generic
combination of $m$ variables $V(\omega)$, is non-negative if $m$
is odd and non-positive if $m$ is even.
\end{enumerate}
Following \citet{ben1985discrete}, if $\xi_{\iota}(\omega)$'s (the
idiosyncratic taste parameters) are drawn from the following distribution
\[
F_{k}(\boldsymbol{\xi})=\exp\left(-H_{k}(\exp(\boldsymbol{\xi}))\right)=\exp\left(-\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}\left(\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)}A(\varphi)\exp(\xi(\omega))^{\theta_{k}}\right)^{\gamma_{k}/\theta_{k}}\right),
\]
then the probability of choosing variety $\omega\in\Omega_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$,
namely, $\lambda(\omega)\equiv\lambda\left(Y,\tilde{p}_{i,k},p_{\omega i},\varphi\right)$
is given by
\begin{align*}
\lambda(\omega) & =\frac{V(\omega)\frac{\partial H_{k}(\boldsymbol{V})}{\partial V(\omega)}}{\gamma_{k}H_{k}(\boldsymbol{V})}=\frac{A(\varphi)V(\omega)^{\theta_{k}}\ \left(\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)}A(\varphi)V(\omega')^{\theta_{k}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}-1}}{\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}\left(\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{i,k}\left(\varphi',y\right)}A(\varphi')V(\omega')^{\theta_{k}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}}}\\
 & =\frac{V(\omega)^{\theta_{k}}}{\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)}V(\omega')^{\theta_{k}}}\cdot\frac{\left(A(\varphi)\ \sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)}V(\omega')^{\theta_{k}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}}}{\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}\left(A(\varphi')\ \sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(\varphi',y\right)}V(\omega')^{\theta_{k}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}}}.
\end{align*}
The expression for $q_{k}\left(.\right)$ follows trivially from the
above expression by integrating over all consumers in market $i$. 

\subsection{\label{sec:Proof-Lemma2}Demand Elasticity in Continuous Industries}

This appendix derives the demand elasticity in continuous industries,
which amounts to proving Lemma 2 from Appendix \ref{sec: Non-Parametric-Model}.
Claim (a) in Lemma 2 can be proven by taking the derivative of $q_{k}\left(.\right)$
w.r.t. $p_{ji,k}(\omega)$:
\begin{align*}
\hspace{-1in}\frac{\partial q_{k}\left(p_{ji,k}(\omega),...\right)}{\partial p_{ji,k}(\omega)}= & \frac{\partial}{\partial p_{ji,k}(\omega)}\left[\int_{y}\mathcal{D}_{k}\left(e_{k}yw_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)\lambda_{k}\left(y,e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}(y)\right)dG_{i}\left(y\right)\right]L_{i}\\
\hspace{-1in}= & \left[\int_{y}\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{D}_{k}\left(.\right)}{\partial p_{ji,k}(\omega)}\lambda_{k}\left(y,e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi;\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}(y)\right)+\mathcal{D}_{k}\left(e_{k}yw_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)\frac{\partial\lambda_{k}\left(.\right)}{\partial p_{ji,k}(\omega)}\right)dG_{i}\left(y\right)\right]L_{i}\\
\hspace{-1in}= & -\left[\int_{y}\frac{1}{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}\left(1+\theta_{k}\frac{e_{k}yw_{i}}{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}\frac{v_{k}'\left(e_{k}yw_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)}{v_{k}\left(e_{k}yw_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)}\right)\mathcal{D}_{k}\left(e_{k}yw_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)\lambda_{k}\left(.\right)dG_{i}\left(y\right)\right]L_{i}\\
\hspace{-1in}= & -\frac{q_{k}\left(.\right)}{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}\left[1+\theta_{k}\int_{y}\frac{e_{k}yw_{i}}{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}\frac{v_{k}'\left(yw_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)}{v_{k}\left(yw_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)}d\mathcal{G}_{i,k}\left(y,w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi;\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\right)\right],
\end{align*}
where \emph{$\mathcal{G}_{i,k}$ }denotes the\emph{ demand-weighted}
income distribution, which augments the actual income distribution,
$G_{i}\left(.\right)$, by weighing each income group by their demand:
\[
d\mathcal{G}_{i,k}\left(y,w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi;\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\right)\equiv\frac{\lambda_{k}\left(y,e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}(y)\right)dG_{i}\left(y\right)}{\int_{y'}\lambda_{k}\left(y,e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}(y')\right)\cdot dG_{i}\left(y'\right)}\cdot
\]
Using the above expressions, we can immediately calculate the demand
elasticity, $\varepsilon_{k}\left(.\right)=\mid\partial\ln q_{k}\left(.\right)/\partial\ln p_{ji,k}(\omega)\mid$,
as follows:
\[
\varepsilon_{k}\left(e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi;\boldsymbol{P}_{i},G_{i}\right)=1+\theta_{k}\left[\int_{y}\frac{v_{k}'\left(ye_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)}{v_{k}\left(ye_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)}\ y\ d\mathcal{G}_{i,k}\left(y;e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi)\right)\right]\frac{e_{k}w_{i}}{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}.
\]
The above equation clearly states that apart from the aggregate demand
shifters, $\boldsymbol{P}_{i}$, the income distribution, $G_{i}\left(.\right)$,
and the quality level, $\varphi$, which applies to all firms in set
$\Omega_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right)$, $\varepsilon_{k}\left(.\right)$
only depends on the average demand level, $e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega)$.

To prove Claim (b), I first need to characterize the conditions under
which $\lambda_{k}\left(.\right)$ is invariant to income. To this
end, defining $x_{ji,k}(\omega)\equiv e_{k}y/p_{ji,k}(\omega)$, we
can take the derivative of $\lambda_{k}\left(.\right)$ as follows:
\begin{align}
\hspace{-0.75in}\frac{\partial\ln\lambda_{k}\left(x_{\omega},\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\right)}{\partial\ln y}= & \theta_{k}\left(\frac{\partial\ln v_{k}\left(x_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)}{\partial\ln y}\ -\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(y,\varphi\right)}\frac{\partial\ln v_{k}\left(x_{ji,k}(\omega')\right)}{\partial\ln y}\frac{\lambda_{k}\left(x_{ji,k}(\omega'),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\right)}{\Lambda_{k}\left(\varphi,y\right)}\right)\label{eq: Lemma 2 -- part b}\\
\hspace{-0.75in}- & \gamma_{k}\left[\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(y,\varphi\right)}\frac{\partial\ln v_{k}\left(x_{ji,k}(\omega')\right)}{\partial\ln y}\frac{\lambda_{k}\left(x_{ji,k}(\omega'),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\right)}{\Lambda_{k}\left(\varphi,y\right)}\right.\nonumber \\
\hspace{-0.75in} & -\left.\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(y,\varphi\right)}x_{ji,k}(\omega')\frac{\partial\ln v_{k}\left(x_{ji,k}(\omega')\right)}{\partial\ln y}\lambda_{k}\left(x_{ji,k}(\omega'),\varphi',\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\right)\right],\nonumber 
\end{align}
where $\Lambda_{k}\left(\varphi,y\right)\equiv P_{i,k}(\varphi,y)^{-\gamma_{k}}/\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}\left[P_{i,k}(\varphi',y)^{-\gamma_{k}}\right]$
denotes the share of consumers choosing quality $\varphi$. Given
that the probability shares add up to one, i.e.,
\[
\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(y,\varphi\right)}\lambda_{k}\left(x_{ji,k}(\omega'),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\right)/\Lambda_{k}\left(\varphi,y\right)=\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}\sum_{\omega'\in\Omega_{j,k}\left(y,\varphi\right)}\lambda_{k}\left(x_{ji,k}(\omega'),\varphi',\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\right)=1,
\]
a sufficient condition for $\partial\ln\lambda_{k}\left(.\right)/\partial y=0$
is that $\partial\ln v_{k}\left(x\right)/\partial\ln y=\textrm{constant}$.
Given that $x\equiv ey/p$, this condition can be otherwise stated
as
\[
xv_{k}'\left(x\right)/v_{k}\left(x\right)=c_{k},
\]
where $c_{k}$ is an industry-level constant. It follows trivially
from Equation \ref{eq: Lemma 2 -- part b} that the above condition
is also necessary for the invariance of $\lambda_{k}\left(.\right)$
w.r.t. $y$. In particular, if $\partial\ln\lambda_{k}\left(x_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\right)/\partial\ln y=0$
is to be satisfied simultaneously for all $\omega$, then it should
be the case that $xv_{k}'\left(x\right)/v_{k}\left(x\right)=c_{k}$.
Plugging this condition into the general demand elasticity formula,
yields the constant elasticity expression:
\[
\varepsilon_{k}\left(e_{k}w_{i}/p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi;\boldsymbol{P}_{i},G_{i}\right)=1+\theta_{k}c_{k},
\]
where the formula stated under Lemma 2 concerns the special case,
where $c_{k}=1$.

\subsection{\label{sec: Proof-Lemma3}Demand Elasticity in Discrete Industries}

Claim (a) can be proven by applying the Leibniz integral rule as follows:
\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial q_{k}\left(p_{ji,k}(\omega),...\right)}{\partial p_{ji,k}(\omega)} & =-\lambda_{k}\left(\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}},p_{ji,k}(\omega),\tilde{p}_{i,k},\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\left(y\right)\right)g_{i}\left(p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)L_{i}/e_{k}w_{i}+\\
 & -\frac{\theta_{k}}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}}\left(\int_{\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}}}^{\infty}\frac{v_{k}'\left(y\frac{e_{k}w_{i}}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}}-\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}}\right)}{v_{k}\left(y\frac{e_{k}w_{i}}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}}-\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}}\right)}\lambda_{k}\left(y,p_{ji,k}(\omega),\tilde{p}_{i,k},\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\left(y\right)\right)dG_{i}(y)\right)L_{i}.
\end{align*}
where, as defined in the mains text, $\overline{\lambda}_{k}(p_{ji,k}(\omega),\tilde{p}_{i},\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\left(y\right))\equiv q_{k}\left(.\right)/\left[1-G_{i}\left(p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)\right]L_{i}$
denotes the purchase probability of the average consumer who can afford
$\omega$. Recalling the definition of $\mathcal{G}_{i,k}\left(.\right)$
from Appendix \ref{sec:Proof-Lemma2}, the above equation immediately
implies the following expression for the demand elasticity, $\varepsilon_{k}\left(.\right)=\mbox{\ensuremath{\mid\partial\ln q_{k}\left(.\right)}/\ensuremath{\partial\ln p_{ji,k}}(\ensuremath{\omega})\ensuremath{\mid}}$:
\begin{align*}
\hspace{-0.8in}\varepsilon_{k}\left(\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}},\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}},\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i},G_{i}\right)= & \left[\frac{\lambda_{k}\left(\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}},\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}},\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\left(y\right)\right)}{\overline{\lambda}_{k}(p_{ji,k}(\omega),\varphi,\tilde{p}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\left(y\right))}\frac{g_{i}(p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i})}{1-G_{i}\left(p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)}\right]\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}}\\
\hspace{-0.8in}+ & \theta_{k}\left[\int_{\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}}}^{\infty}\frac{v_{k}'\left(\tilde{e}_{i,k}y-\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}}\right)}{v_{k}\left(\tilde{e}_{i,k}y-\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}}\right)}d\mathcal{G}_{i,k}\left(y;\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}},\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i}\right)\right]\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}},
\end{align*}
where $\tilde{e}_{k}\equiv e_{k}/\tilde{a}_{i,k}$. The above equation
clearly states that apart from the aggregate demand shifters, $\boldsymbol{P}_{i}$,
the income distribution, $G_{i}\left(.\right)$, and the quality level,
$\varphi$, which applies to all firms in set $\Omega_{j,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$,
$\varepsilon_{k}\left(.\right)$ only depends on $(i)$ the degree
of affordability $p_{ji,k}(\omega)/e_{k}w_{i}$, and $(ii)$ the price
relative to services, $p_{ji,k}(\omega)/\tilde{p}_{i,k}$.

To prove Claim (b), I first need to characterize the conditions under
which $\lambda_{k}\left(.\right)$ is invariant to income. To this
end, we can take the same exact steps outlined earlier in the proof
of Lemma 2, which imply that individual demand probabilities are (conditionally)
invariant to $y$ iff $\partial\ln v_{k}\left(x\right)/\partial\ln y=\textrm{constant}$.
In the case of discrete demand industries, where $x=\left(y-p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)/\tilde{p}_{i,k}$,
this condition simply reduces to
\[
v_{k}'\left(x\right)/v_{k}\left(x\right)=c_{k},
\]
where $c_{k}$ is an industry-level constant. Plugging this condition
into the general demand elasticity formula, yields the following formulation:
\[
\varepsilon_{k}\left(p_{\omega i}/e_{k}w_{i},p_{ji,k}(\omega)/\tilde{p}_{i,k},\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i},G_{i}\right)=c_{k}\theta_{k}\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}}\ +\ \rho_{ji,k}(\omega)\mathcal{H}_{i}(\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}})\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}},
\]
where $\mathcal{H}_{i}\left(y\right)=g_{i}\left(y\right)/\left(1-G_{i}\left(y\right)\right)$
the hazard rate of the income distribution in market $i$. Also, note
that the formula stated under Lemma 3 concerns the special case, where
$c_{k}=1$. The demand elasticity in benchmark model presented in
\ref{sec:Theoretical-Framework} can be attained as a special case
of the above formula, where $(i)$ $c_{k}=1$, and $(ii)$ the endowment
distribution is exponential, with a constant hazard rate $\mathcal{H}_{i}(.)=\zeta_{i}$.
So, given that $\rho_{ji,k}(\omega)=\rho_{ji,k}\left(p_{ji,k}(\omega)\right)\approx1$
to a first-order approximation, the above elasticity formula in this
special case reduces to Equation \ref{eq: Eq epsilon} from Section
\ref{sec:Theoretical-Framework}:
\[
\varepsilon_{ji,k}(\varphi)=\theta_{k}\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{\tilde{p}_{i,k}}\ +\ \zeta_{i}\frac{p_{ji,k}(\omega)}{e_{k}w_{i}}.
\]


\subsection{\label{sec: Deriving-Equation for QS}Deriving Equation \ref{eq: IQS}}

\paragraph*{Continuous industries ($k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}$):}

In the case of continuous industries, the CES demand implies that
\[
\text{\ensuremath{\frac{Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)}{Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)}}}=1\Longleftrightarrow\text{\ensuremath{\frac{p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)}{p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)}}}=1,\ \ \ k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}.
\]
The right-hand side of the above condition holds due to the assumption
price exhibits a constant markup and the country-specific cost-shifter
is quality-neutral: $p_{ji,k}=\mu_{k}\tau_{ji,k}a_{j,k}c(\varphi)w_{i}$.

\paragraph*{Discrete industries ($k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}$):}

The demand facing a firm supplying discrete varieties from country
$j$ to market $i$ is given by:
\begin{equation}
q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)=\left[\int_{\frac{p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)}{e_{k}w_{i}}}^{\infty}\exp\left(-p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)/\theta_{k}\right)\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)e^{-\zeta_{i}\left(y-\chi_{i}\right)}dy\right]\ \ \ \varphi\in\varPhi_{k},\label{eq: appendix demand homo.}
\end{equation}
In the above equation, $\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$ is a
\emph{quality$\times$income}-specific demand shifters, which can
be expressed as follows:
\[
\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)=\frac{\left[\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}N_{\ell,k}(\varphi)\exp\left(-p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)/\theta_{k}\right)\right]^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}-1}}{\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}\left[\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}N_{\ell,k}(\varphi)\exp\left(-p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)/\theta_{k}\right)\right]^{\frac{\gamma_{k}}{\theta_{k}}}}L_{i}.
\]
Since, $\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)$ is piecewise differentiable
with $\partial\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)/\partial y=0$,
we can perform integration by parts (pice-by-piece) to re-write Equation
\ref{eq: appendix demand homo.} as follows:
\begin{align*}
q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right) & =\exp\left(-p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)/\tilde{p}_{i}\theta_{k}\right)\left[\frac{1}{\zeta_{i}}e^{-\zeta_{i}\left(\frac{p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)}{e_{k}w_{i}}-\bar{y}_{i}\right)}\right]\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi,p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)\\
 & =A_{i}\ \exp\left(p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)/w_{i}\right)^{-\vartheta_{i,k}}\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi,p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)/e_{k}w_{i}\right),
\end{align*}
where $1/\vartheta_{i,k}\equiv\theta_{k}/\tilde{a}_{i}+\zeta_{i}/e_{k}$
and $A_{i}\equiv e^{\zeta_{i}\bar{y}_{i}}/\zeta_{i}$. Noting that
$(i)$ $Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)=N_{j,k}\left(\varphi\right)q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)$
and $(ii)$ $p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)=\tau_{ji,k}a_{j,k}w_{j}c_{k}\left(\varphi\right)+\vartheta_{i,k}w_{i}$
, the above equation yields the following expression:
\begin{align}
\frac{Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)}{Q_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)} & =\frac{N_{j,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)}{N_{j,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)}\exp\left(\left[p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)-p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)\right]\right)^{\frac{\vartheta_{i,k}}{w_{i}}}\frac{\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi_{H},p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)}{\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi_{L},p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)}\nonumber \\
 & =\frac{N_{j,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)}{N_{j,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)}\exp\left(\left[c_{k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)-c_{k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)\right]\tau_{ji,k}a_{j,k}w_{j}\right)^{\frac{\vartheta_{i,k}}{w_{i}}}\frac{\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi_{H},p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)}{\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi_{L},p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)}.\label{eq: appendix demand homo 2}
\end{align}
Finally, given that to a first-order approximation $\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi,y\right)=\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi,\bar{y}_{i}\right)$
for all $y$, then for any two suppliers $j$ and $\ell$,
\[
\frac{\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi_{H},p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)/\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi_{L},p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)}{\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi_{H},p_{\ell i,k}\left(\varphi_{H}\right)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)/\varPsi_{i,k}\left(\varphi_{L},p_{\ell i,k}\left(\varphi_{L}\right)/e_{k}w_{i}\right)}\approx1.
\]
That being the case, Equation \ref{eq: appendix demand homo 2} immediately
implies Expression \ref{eq: IQS} for $k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}$.

\subsection{\label{subsec: Proof Proposition 2}Proof of Proposition 2}

Let $r_{ji,k}(\varphi)=Q_{ji,k}(\varphi)/\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}Q_{ji,k}(\varphi')$
and let us only focus on a discrete industry $k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}$.
An immediate corollary of Equation \ref{eq: IQS} (derived in the
previous appendix) is that for any $\varphi_{H}$ and $\varphi_{L}\in\varPhi_{k}$
such that $\varphi_{H}>\varphi_{L}$:
\[
\frac{\partial r_{ji,k}(\varphi_{H})/r_{ji,k}(\varphi_{L})}{\partial\tilde{p}_{i}},\ \frac{\partial r_{ji,k}(\varphi_{H})/r_{ji,k}(\varphi_{L})}{\partial\tilde{p}_{j}},\ \frac{\partial r_{ji,k}(\varphi_{H})/r_{ji,k}(\varphi_{L})}{\partial a_{j,k}}>0.
\]
Combining the above relationship with the fact that $\sum_{\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}}r_{ji,k}(\varphi)=1$,
the above expression simply implies that
\[
\frac{\partial^{2}r_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{\partial\varphi\partial\tilde{p}_{i}},\ \frac{\partial^{2}r_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{\partial\varphi\partial\tilde{p}_{j}},\ \frac{\partial^{2}r_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{\partial\varphi\partial a_{j,k}}>0.
\]
Now let us focus on the effect of $\tilde{p}_{i}$ on the aggregate
export unit price, $\bar{p}_{ji,k}$. Given that $(a)$ $\frac{\partial p_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{\partial\tilde{p}_{i}}$,
$(b)$ $\frac{\partial p_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{\partial\varphi}>0$, and
$(c)$ $\frac{\partial^{2}r_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{\partial\varphi\partial\tilde{p}_{i}}>0$,
it immediately follows that
\[
\frac{\partial\bar{p}_{ji,k}}{\partial\tilde{p}_{i}}=\sum_{\varphi'\in\varPhi_{k}}\left(p_{ji,k}(\varphi)\frac{\partial r_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{\partial\tilde{p}_{i}}+\frac{\partial p_{ji,k}(\varphi)}{\partial\tilde{p}_{i}}r_{ji,k}(\varphi\right))>0,\ \ \ k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}.
\]
Along the same line arguments we can establish that $\frac{\partial\bar{p}_{ji,k}}{\partial\tilde{p}_{j}}>0$
and $\frac{\partial\bar{\varphi}_{ji,k}}{\partial a_{j,k}}>0$ if
$k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}$. Meanwhile, the fact $\frac{\partial\bar{p}_{ji,k}}{\partial\tilde{p}_{i}}=\frac{\partial\bar{p}_{ji,k}}{\partial\tilde{p}_{j}}=0$
if $k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}}$ follows trivially from all components
of $r_{ji,k}(\varphi)$ and $p_{ji,k}(\varphi)$ being invariant to$\tilde{p}_{j}$,
$\tilde{p}_{i}$. Relatedly, $\frac{\partial\bar{\varphi}_{ji,k}}{\partial a_{j,k}}=0$
follows from $r_{ji,k}(\varphi)$ being invariant to $a_{j,k}$.

\subsection{\label{subsec: GT Derivation}Gains from Trade Formulas}

This appendix derives the gains from trade formula presented in Section
\ref{sec: GT} under Equation \ref{eq: GT one-sector}. Recall that
this equation is derived under the assumption that $(a)$ the traded
sector is entirely discrete (labeled $\mathcal{D}$), and $(b)$ consumers
spend $e_{i,\mathcal{D}}$ of their total budget on consumption categories
where traded discrete goods are combined with non-traded services.
Based on these assumptions, Equation \ref{eq: GT} implies that
\[
GT_{i}=1-\left(\lambda_{ii,\mathcal{D}}/\hat{N}_{i,\mathcal{D}}\right)^{\frac{e_{i,\mathcal{D}}}{\theta}}.
\]
To arrive at Equation \ref{eq: GT one-sector} from the above expression,
we need to characterize $\hat{N}_{i,\mathcal{D}}$. To this end, we
can appeal to the free-entry condition:
\[
N_{i,\mathcal{D}}w_{i}f^{e}=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}(p_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}-c_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}})Q_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}.
\]
where $Q_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}=\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}L_{\ell}$.
In the absence of affordability constraints, $p_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}=c_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}+w_{\ell}/\tilde{a}_{\ell}\theta$.
Assuming $\tilde{a}_{\ell}=1$ for all $\ell$, and substituting for
$p_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}-c_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}$ in the above expression
yields
\[
N_{i,\mathcal{D}}w_{i}f^{e}=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\frac{w_{\ell}}{\theta}\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}L_{\ell}=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\left(\frac{1}{\theta}\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}\frac{w_{\ell}L_{\ell}}{w_{i}L_{i}}\right)w_{i}L_{i}.
\]
Rearranging the above equation implies, $N_{i,\mathcal{D}}=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\left(\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}\frac{w_{\ell}L_{\ell}}{w_{i}L_{i}}\right)\frac{L_{i}}{\theta f^{e}}$.
Accordingly, under autarky, $N_{i,\mathcal{D}}^{A}=\frac{L_{i}}{\theta f^{e}}$,
which yields 
\[
\hat{N}_{i,\mathcal{D}}=N_{i,\mathcal{D}}^{A}/N_{i,\mathcal{D}}=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}\left(\lambda_{i\ell,\mathcal{D}}\frac{w_{\ell}L_{\ell}}{w_{i}L_{i}}\right).
\]
Plugging the above expression back in to expression for $GT_{i}$,
yields \ref{eq: GT one-sector}.

\subsection{\label{subsec: Equation 17}Derivation of Equation \ref{eq: N_i,D}}

As shown in the previous appendix, we can write the (Free Entry) equation
for country $1$ as follows:
\begin{align}
N_{1,\mathcal{D}} & =\left(\lambda_{12,\mathcal{D}}\frac{w_{2}L_{2}}{w_{1}L_{1}}+\lambda_{11,\mathcal{D}}\frac{w_{1}L_{1}}{w_{1}L_{1}}\right)\frac{L_{1}}{\theta f^{e}}=\left(\lambda_{12,\mathcal{D}}\frac{w_{2}L_{2}}{w_{1}L_{1}}+\lambda_{11,\mathcal{D}}\right)\frac{L_{1}}{\theta f^{e}}\label{eq: N1_D}
\end{align}
Rearranging the (Balanced Trade) equation, the term $\lambda_{12,\mathcal{D}}\frac{w_{2}L_{2}}{w_{1}L_{1}}$
(in Equation \ref{eq: N1_D}) can be alternatively expressed as
\begin{align*}
\lambda_{12,\mathcal{D}}\frac{w_{2}L_{2}}{w_{1}L_{1}} & =\left(\frac{\tau a\frac{w_{2}}{w_{1}}+\frac{1}{\theta}}{\tau a\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}+\frac{1}{\theta}}\right)\lambda_{21,\mathcal{D}}\\
 & =\lambda_{21,\mathcal{D}}\left[1+\frac{\tau a\frac{w_{2}}{w_{1}}-\tau a\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}}{\tau a\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}+\frac{1}{\theta}}\right]=\lambda_{21,\mathcal{D}}\left[1+\frac{\frac{w_{2}}{w_{1}}-\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}}{\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}+\frac{1}{\tau a\theta}}\right].
\end{align*}
Plugging the above expression for $\lambda_{12,\mathcal{D}}\frac{w_{2}L_{2}}{w_{1}L_{1}}$
back into Equation \ref{eq: N1_D} yields the following expression
for $N_{1,\mathcal{D}}$:
\begin{align}
N_{1,\mathcal{D}} & =\left(\lambda_{21,\mathcal{D}}\left[1+\frac{\frac{w_{2}}{w_{1}}-\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}}{\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}+\frac{1}{\tau a\theta}}\right]+\lambda_{11,\mathcal{D}}\right)\frac{L_{1}}{\theta f^{e}}=\left(1+\frac{\frac{w_{2}}{w_{1}}-\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}}{\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}+\frac{1}{\tau a\theta}}\lambda_{21,\mathcal{D}}\right)\frac{L_{1}}{\theta f^{e}},\label{eq: N1_D NEW}
\end{align}
where the second line follows from $\lambda_{21,\mathcal{D}}+\lambda_{11,\mathcal{D}}=1$.
Following the same exact steps, we can derive the following expression
for $N_{2,D}$:
\begin{equation}
N_{2,\mathcal{D}}=\left(1+\frac{\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}-\frac{w_{2}}{w_{1}}}{\frac{w_{2}}{w_{1}}+\frac{1}{\tau a\theta}}\lambda_{21,\mathcal{D}}\right)\frac{L_{2}}{\theta f^{e}}.\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \label{eq: N2_D NEW}
\end{equation}
Equations \ref{eq: N1_D NEW} and \ref{eq: N2_D NEW} can be alternatively
formulated as
\[
N_{i,\mathcal{D}}=\left(1+\frac{\frac{w_{-i}}{w_{i}}-\frac{w_{i}}{w_{-i}}}{\frac{w_{i}}{w_{-i}}+\frac{1}{a\tau\theta}}\lambda_{-ii,\mathcal{D}}\right)\frac{L_{i}}{\theta f^{e}}.
\]


\section{\label{sec: Discrete-Trade-with-Firm-Het}Discrete Trade with Firm-Level
Heterogeneity}

Below, I outline the implications of firm-heterogeneity for the model.
Before doing so, note that the firm-level predictions of the model,
with regards to PTM, are not sensitive to firm-level heterogeneity
by construction. The macro-level predictions, regarding IQS, however,
can change with the introduction of firm heterogeneity. 

In the baseline model, $c_{k}(\varphi,z$) denotes the marginal labor
requirement for producing quality $\varphi$ in industry $k$. In
the baseline case, $z$ differs across countries but is the same across
all firms in a given country. So, to model firm heterogeneity I make
the following amendments to the baseline model:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Firms are ex-ante identical in industry $k$. After paying the entry
cost, firms are assigned a productivity, $z$, which is the realization
of a random variable drawn independently across firms from a Pareto
distribution:
\[
F_{j,k}\left(z\right)=1-A_{j,k}z^{-\eta_{k}},
\]
where $A_{j,k}$ is a country$\times$industry-specific productivity
shifter.
\item Firms have to incur a fixed cost, $f_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right)$,
to serve market $i$ in quality level $\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}$.
\end{enumerate}
Extending the discussion in Appendix \ref{sec: Non-Parametric-Model},
the profits facing each firm with productivity $z$ can be expressed
as $\pi_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,z\right),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\right)$,
where $\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,z\right)\equiv p_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,z\right)/w_{i}$.
The zero-profit cutoff is, therefore, determined by the following
equation:
\[
\pi_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}^{*}\left(\varphi,z\right),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\right)=w_{i}f_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right).
\]
Importantly, the above equation implies that $\nu_{ji,k}^{*}\left(\varphi,z\right)$
should be uniform across all exporting countries. Namely,
\[
\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,z_{ji,k}^{*}\left(\varphi\right)\right)\equiv\nu_{i,k}^{*}\left(\varphi\right).
\]
Correspondingly, the total value of exports from country $j$ to market
$i$ in quality-level $\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}$ is given by
\begin{equation}
X_{ji,k}\left(\varphi\right)=N_{j,k}\left(\varphi\right)\left(\int_{z_{ji}^{*}\left(\varphi\right)}^{\infty}\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,z\right)\lambda_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,z\right),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\right)w_{i}L_{i}\ \text{d}F_{j,k}\left(z\right)\right)w_{i}L_{i}.\label{eq: Xji Firm-Het}
\end{equation}
To present the next step transparently, let $m_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,z\right),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\right)\equiv\varepsilon/\varepsilon-1$
denote the markup charged by a firm with characteristics $\left(\varphi,z\right)$,
exporting industry $k$ goods from country $j$ to market $i$. Then,
by definition, $m_{k}\left(\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,z\right),\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\right)w_{j}\tau_{ji}c_{k}\left(\varphi\right)/w_{i}z=\nu_{ji,k}\left(\varphi,z\right)$;
and we can write $\text{d}\ln z$ in terms of $\text{d}\ln\nu$ as
follows
\[
\text{d}\ln z=\left(1+\frac{\partial\ln m_{k}}{\partial\ln\nu}\right)\text{d}\ln\nu.
\]
The above expression, in turn, implies that
\[
\text{d}z=\frac{w_{j}\tau_{ji}}{w_{i}}\frac{c_{k}\left(\varphi\right)m_{k}\left(\nu,\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\right)}{\nu\left(1+\frac{\partial\ln m_{k}}{\partial\ln\nu}\right)^{-1}}\frac{\text{d}\nu}{\nu}.
\]
Given the Pareto productivity distribution, the above equation yields
the following formulation for $dF_{j,k}\left(z\right)$:
\begin{align*}
dF_{j,k}\left(z\right)= & \eta_{k}A_{j,k}z^{-\eta_{k}-1}\text{d}z\\
= & \eta_{k}A_{j,k}\left(\frac{w_{j}\tau_{ji}}{w_{i}}\frac{c_{k}\left(\varphi\right)m_{k}\left(\nu,\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\right)}{\nu\left(1+\frac{\partial\ln m_{k}}{\partial\ln\nu}\right)^{-1}}\right)^{-\eta_{k}}\frac{\text{d}\nu}{\nu}.
\end{align*}
Plugging the above equation back into Equation \ref{eq: Xji Firm-Het},
yields the following expression for $X_{ji}\left(\varphi\right)$:
\[
X_{ji}\left(\varphi\right)=\psi_{k}A_{j,k}N_{j}\left(\varphi\right)\left(\frac{\tau_{ji,k}w_{j}}{w_{i}}\right)^{-\eta_{k}}w_{i}L_{i}\mathcal{Q}_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right),
\]
where
\[
\mathcal{Q}_{i,k}\left(\varphi\right)\equiv\int_{0}^{\nu_{i,k}^{*}\left(\varphi\right)}\lambda_{k}\left(\nu,\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\right)\left[\frac{c_{k}\left(\varphi\right)m_{k}\left(\nu,\varphi,\boldsymbol{P}_{i,k}\right)}{\nu\left(1+\frac{\partial\ln m_{k}}{\partial\ln\nu}\right)^{-1}}\right]^{-\eta_{k}}\text{d}\ensuremath{\nu},
\]
depends only on the characteristics of the importing market, $i$.
Letting $E_{i}\left(\varphi\right)$ denote the total expenditure
on quality $\varphi\in\varPhi_{k}$, the budget constraint of consumers
in market $i$ entails that $\sum_{j\in\mathbb{C}}X_{ji}\left(\varphi\right)=E_{i}\left(\varphi\right)$.
This condition plus the above equation, imply the following gravity
equation describing macro-level export values:
\[
X_{ji}\left(\varphi\right)=\frac{A_{j,k}N_{j}\left(\varphi\right)\left(\tau_{ji,k}w_{j}\right)^{-\eta_{k}}}{\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{C}}A_{\ell,k}N_{\ell}\left(\varphi\right)\left(\tau_{\ell i,k}w_{\ell}\right)^{-\eta_{k}}}E_{i}\left(\varphi\right).
\]
Considering the above expression, the prediction of model regarding
the \emph{home-market driven} quality specialization remains intact.
That is, high-wage countries, which have a greater home-market demand
for quality, would host a greater number of high-quality producing
firms. Accordingly, due to their higher $N_{j}\left(\varphi\right)$
in high-quality (high-$\varphi$) categories, they would export relatively
more high-quality goods. However, based on the above equation, the
prediction that affordability constraints induce IQS no longer holds.
One should nonetheless keep in mind that the break-down of affordability-driven
IQS is a mere artifact of the Pareto assumption, rather than firm
heterogeneity per se.

\section{\label{sec:Additional-Test-the}Additional Test the Model}

Section \ref{sec:Empirical-Evidence} tested Proposition 2 while restricting
the \noun{Baci} dataset to sub-samples of \emph{$(i)$ }only\emph{
final goods} and $(ii)$ only \emph{differentiated} \emph{goods} .
In this appendix I present an alternative test that groups HS6 product
by their underlying demand elasticity. To this end, I use the estimated
elasticities by \citet{Broda2006}. I classify HS6 products as less-
and more- differentiated based on the following criteria:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{More-differentiated} HS6 products exhibit a lower-or-equal-to-median
elasticity, i.e., $\sigma_{BW}\leq3.6$.
\item \emph{Less-differentiated} HS6 products exhibit an above-median demand
elasticity, i.e., $\sigma_{BW}>3.6$. 
\end{enumerate}
I then re-estimate Equation \ref{eq: Baci Regression} separately
on these two sub-groups of products. The estimation results are reported
in Table \ref{tab:price-regression-robust_BW}, and corroborate the
model's prediction that export price levels --in discrete product
categories-- vary systematically with the price of non-traded services
in the origin and destination economy as well the origin economy's
degree of comparative advantage. At the same time, these same patterns
are either non-existent or weaker in continuous product categories---refer
to Section \ref{sec:Empirical-Evidence} for a more elaborate discussion
of these predictions.

\section{\label{sec:Estimation-of-theta}Estimation of $\theta$}

This appendix describes how the triple difference procedure developed
by \citet{caliendo2014estimates} can be employed to estimate $\theta$.
This procedure relies on applied tariff data. So, before outlining
the procedure, I describe how the data on applied tariffs is compiled. 

\paragraph*{The UNCTAD-TRAINS Data}

The United Nations Statistical Division, Trade Analysis and Information
System (UNCTAD-TRAINS) reports data on applied tariff for 2008, spanning
31 two-digit (in ISIC rev.3) sectors, 181 importers, and 245 export
partners. In line with \citet{caliendo2014estimates}, I use the \emph{simple
tariff line average} of the \emph{effectively applied tariff} (AHS)
denoting it by $t_{ji,k}$. In instances where tariff data are missing
for 2008, I use tariff data for the nearest available year, giving
priority to earlier years. To aggregate the UNCTAD-TRAINS data into
individual WIOD industries, I closely follow the methodology outlined
in \citet{kucheryavyy2016grounded}. Importantly, individual European
Union (EU) member countries are not represented in the UNCTAD-TRAINS
data during the 2000-2014 period. So, I infer their applied tariff
rates from applied EU tariffs, given that intra-EU trade is subject
to zero tariffs while all EU members impose a common external tariff
on non-members.

\paragraph*{Continuous Model.}

Equation \ref{eq: expenditure share}, bilateral trade shares in continuous
traded industries can be characterized as
\[
\lambda_{ji,k}=N_{j,k}\Omega_{i,k}\left[c_{ji,k}(1+t_{ji,k})\right]{}^{-\theta}\ \ \ k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{C}},
\]
where $\Omega_{i,k}\equiv\sum_{n}\left(N_{n,k}\left[c_{ni,k}(1+t_{ni,k})\right]{}^{-\theta}\right)e_{i,k}$
can be treated as an importer$\times$industry fixed effect, and $c_{ji,k}$
denotes the marginal cost of producing and transporting industry $k$
goods from origin $j$ to destination $i$. Suppose $\ln c_{ji,k}=\ln\nu_{j,k}+\ln d_{ji,k}+\varepsilon_{ji,k}$,
where $d_{ji,k}=d_{ij,k}$ is a systematic and symmetric component
that accounts for the cost-equivalent effect of distance, common language,
and common border, and $\varepsilon_{ji,k}$ is a random disturbance
term that represents deviation from symmetry. Using this decomposition,
we can produce the following estimating equation for any triplet $(j,i,n)$:
\[
\ln\frac{\lambda_{ji,k}\lambda_{in,k}\lambda_{nj,k}}{\lambda_{ij,k}\lambda_{ni,k}\lambda_{jn,k}}=-\theta\ln\frac{(1+t_{ji,k})(1+t_{in,k})(1+t_{nj})}{(1+t_{ij,k})(1+t_{ni,k})(1+t_{jn,k})}+\tilde{\varepsilon}_{jin,k},
\]
where $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{jin,k}\equiv\theta_{k}(\varepsilon_{ij,k}-\varepsilon_{ji,k}+\varepsilon_{in,k}-\varepsilon_{ni,k}+\varepsilon_{nj,k}-\varepsilon_{jn,k})$.
The above equation can be used to attain unbiased and consistent estimates
for $\theta$ under the identifying assumption that $\textrm{Cov}(t_{ji,k},\varepsilon_{ji,k})=0$.
 I estimate the above equation using data on trade shares, $\lambda_{ji,k}$,
from the WIOD and matching data on applied tariffs, $t_{ji,k}$, from
the UNCTAD-TRAINS. As noted earlier, the original WIOD data features
16 traded industries. Since I am interested in attaining an economy-wide
estimate for $\theta$, I perform the estimation while pooling data
across all 16 industries, treating them as continuous.

\paragraph*{Discrete Model.}

Equation \ref{eq: expenditure share}, trade shares in discrete traded
industries can be characterized as:
\[
\lambda_{ji,k}=N_{j,k}\Omega_{i,k}\exp(c_{ji,k}+\bar{t}_{ji,k})^{-\theta/\tilde{p}_{j}},\ \ \ k\in\mathbb{K}_{\mathcal{D}}.
\]
where $\Omega_{i,k}\equiv\sum_{n}\left(N_{n,k}\exp(c_{ni,k}+\bar{t}_{ni,k})^{-\theta/\tilde{p}_{i}}\right)e_{i,k}$
can be once again treated as an importer$\times$industry fixed effect,
and $\bar{t}_{ji,k}$ is the per-unit equivalent of the ad-valorem
tariff rate, $t_{ji,k}$. Suppose $c_{ij,k}/\tilde{p}_{j}=\nu_{j,k}+\delta_{i,k}+d_{ij,k}+\varepsilon_{ij,k}$,
where $d_{ji,k}=d_{ij,k}$ is a systematic and symmetric component
that accounts for the cost-equivalent of distance, common language,
and common border, and $\varepsilon_{ji,k}$ is a random disturbance
term that represents deviation from symmetry. This decomposition produces
the following estimating equation for any triplet $(j,i,n)$:

\[
\ln\frac{\lambda_{ji,k}\lambda_{in,k}\lambda_{nj,k}}{\lambda_{ij,k}\lambda_{ni,k}\lambda_{jn,k}}=-\theta\left[\frac{\bar{t}_{ji,k}}{\tilde{p}_{i}}+\frac{\bar{t}_{in,k}}{\tilde{p}_{n}}+\frac{\bar{t}_{nj,k}}{\tilde{p}_{j}}-\frac{\bar{t}_{ij,k}}{\tilde{p}_{j}}-\frac{\bar{t}_{ni,k}}{\tilde{p}_{i}}-\frac{\bar{t}_{jn,k}}{\tilde{p}_{n}}\right]+\tilde{\varepsilon}_{jin,k},
\]
where $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{jin,k}\equiv\theta_{k}(\varepsilon_{ij,k}-\varepsilon_{ji,k}+\varepsilon_{in,k}-\varepsilon_{ni,k}+\varepsilon_{nj,k}-\varepsilon_{jn,k})$.
The above equation can be used to attain unbiased and consistent estimates
for $\theta$ under the identifying assumption that $\textrm{cov}(t_{ji,k},\varepsilon_{ji,k})=0$.
I estimate the above equation using data on trade shares and applied
tariffs from the the WIOD and UNCTAD-TRAINS. Since I am interested
in attaining an economy-wide estimate for $\theta$, I perform the
estimation while pooling data across the 16 traded WIOD industries,
treating them all as discrete.

\section{\label{sec: Construction-of-Figure}Out-of-Sample Performance of
the Discrete Model}

This appendix investigates the out-of-sample predictive power of the
discrete model that is calibrated to data in Section \ref{sec: GT}.
The data moment of interest is the share of expenditure on traded
versus non-trade sectors. Recall that the model is calibrated to fit
only the total share of expenditure on categories where traded and
non-traded services are bundled in the consumption basket.

In line with my analysis in Section \ref{sec: GT}, suppose the traded
sector consists of only discrete industries. In that case, the $L_{i}$
consumers in economy $i$ purchase in total $\mathcal{Q}_{i}=K\times L_{i}$
units of traded goods across all $K$ industries. Hence, letting $\bar{p}_{i}$
denote the average price of tradable consumption in economy $i$,
the total expenditure on non-traded services can be calculated as
$\widetilde{E}_{i}=w_{i}L_{i}-\bar{p}_{i}\mathcal{Q}_{i}$. Correspondingly,
the \emph{share} of service expenditure is given by
\[
\widetilde{e}_{i}\equiv\frac{\widetilde{E}_{i}}{Y_{i}}=\frac{w_{i}L_{i}-\bar{p}_{i}\mathcal{Q}_{i}}{w_{i}L_{i}}=1-\kappa\frac{p_{i}}{\widetilde{p}_{i}},
\]
where $\kappa\equiv K/\tilde{a}$. Given the above equation and data
on $p_{i}/\tilde{p}_{i}$, we can calculate the model's prediction
with regards to the share of service expenditure as $\ln\widehat{1-\tilde{e}_{i}}=\ln\kappa+\ln p_{i}/\widetilde{p}_{i}$.
The data on $p_{i}/\tilde{p}_{i}$ is readily accessible for 182 countries
from the 2011 ICP data, which was described in Section \ref{sec:Empirical-Evidence}.
The same data also reports the factual share of non-traded service
expenditure, $\tilde{e}_{i}$, for each economy. Using this information,
I contrast the predicted values for $\tilde{e}_{i}$ with factual
values in Figure \ref{fig:International-Expenditure-Share}. Encouragingly,
the discrete model performs remarkably well in predicting the cross-national
variation in service expenditure. Finally, note that by allowing for
$\tilde{a}_{i}$ to be a free-moving parameter, I can perfectly match
$\widetilde{e}_{i}$ in all countries. The gains from trade implied
in that case, though, closely resemble those implied by my benchmark
analysis.

\section{Classification of the WIOD Industries }

This appendix describes my classification of the 35 industries in
the WIOD sample, which is used to compute $e_{i,\mathcal{C}}$ and
$e_{i,\mathcal{D}}$. My classification groups industries into three
different categories:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Traded industries (as classified by \citet{costinot2014trade});
\item Non-traded industries whose services are bundled with traded discrete
goods in the consumption basket; and
\item Other non-traded service industries. 
\end{enumerate}
The assignment of the WIOD industries into these categories is reported
in Table \ref{tab:List-of-industries}. To briefly explain my classification,
consider the industries supplying transportation services (i.e., industries
numbers 23-24 in Table \ref{tab:List-of-industries}). A consumer
may purchase a personal car, jet, or yacht, and spend the rest of
their transportation budget on other types of ground, air, or sea
transportation services that are infeasible to perform with their
personally-acquired transportation device. Similarly, a consumer may
purchase a personal grill or an RV (Recreational Vehicle) and spend
the rest of their food and travel budget on hotel and restaurant services
(i.e, industry number 22 in Table \ref{tab:List-of-industries}).
Similar examples can be constructed for household- and health-related
services (i.e., industries numbers 32-35 in Table \ref{tab:List-of-industries}).
But the same argument cannot be readily extended to real estate services
or services supplying residential water, electricity, and gas. Relatedly,
financial services are classified as solely non-traded, because they
concern a non-repetitive service that has to be frequently customized
to match the consumer's needs on a case-to-case basis.
